Introduction and Conceptual Foundations

The social economy and solidarity economy in Brazil represent a significant alternative to conventional economic models, emphasizing cooperation, self-management, and collective ownership over profit maximization. Often referred to in Portuguese as "economia solidária," this sector comprises enterprises that are collectively owned and democratically managed by their workers, prioritizing social and environmental benefits alongside economic sustainability (Ferrarini et al., 2019). The movement has deep roots in Brazilian social history and has evolved into a recognized public policy field with dedicated government institutions, legal frameworks, and national conferences.

Historical Roots and Emergence

The historical foundations of Brazilian solidarity economy can be traced to the predominance of cooperativism since the early 20th century, which established a tradition of collective economic organization in the country (Ferrarini et al., 2019). However, the contemporary solidarity economy movement emerged specifically in the 1980s during the struggle for re-democratization of the country, arising as a response to the government's neoliberal economic plan guided by the Washington Consensus (North, 2017). Neoliberalism in Brazil was characterized by the restructuring of the world of work, the reconfiguration of international capital accumulation, an extraordinary increase in foreign debt, economic stagnation, and growing unemployment. In this context, many companies went bankrupt, and their workers became unemployed. Brazilian workers reacted to this crisis by recovering insolvent factories and creating productive organizations based on self-management, first as an alternative to unemployment, and later as part of a wider economic, political, and social movement known as the solidarity economy, which amplified calls for democracy to be extended from the political to the economic sphere (North, 2017). The movement drew from diverse political, social, and religious streams, including liberation theology adopted by the progressive wing of the Catholic Church in the 1980s, the Landless Workers' Movement, and various pastoral commissions (North, 2017).

Institutionalization and Public Policy Development

A crucial turning point for the solidarity economy in Brazil came with the election of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in 2002. In June 2003, the government established the National Secretariat for the Solidarity Economy (SENAES) within the Ministry of Labor and Employment, marking the introduction of specific public policies for the solidarity economy at the national level (North, 2017). The creation of SENAES was accompanied by the formation of the Brazilian Forum of Solidarity Economy, which was established in June 2003 at the same time as SENAES, creating a collaborative relationship between civil society and government (SENAES, n.d.). The economist and sociologist Paul Singer (1932-2018) became the first head of SENAES and was one of the pioneers in developing the concept and formulating public policies for solidarity economy during the first Lula administration (Brasil, 2024). The term "solidarity economy" itself was used in a pioneering manner in Brazil in 1996 by Paul Singer in an article published in the newspaper Folha de São Paulo, and the concept later became central to government policy (Motta, 2010, as cited in IPEA, n.d.).

The National Secretariat and Its Evolution

The trajectory of SENAES reflects the broader political dynamics affecting the solidarity economy in Brazil. The secretariat was originally created in 2003 during the first Lula administration to formulate, coordinate, and implement policies for the sector (Platform Cooperativism Consortium, 2026). However, it was dismantled in 2019 under the Bolsonaro government, a period that saw the weakening of public policies aimed at solidarity economy initiatives (Platform Cooperativism Consortium, 2026). The secretariat was reinstated in 2023 under the returning Lula administration, now under the name National Secretariat of Popular and Solidarity Economy, and has since been restructured under the leadership of Gilberto Carvalho (Partido dos Trabalhadores, 2026). This institutional oscillation demonstrates how the solidarity economy in Brazil is closely tied to the political fortunes of different governing coalitions and their respective development models.

Legal Framework: The Paul Singer Law

A landmark achievement for the solidarity economy in Brazil occurred on December 23, 2024, when President Lula sanctioned Law No. 15.068, known as the Paul Singer Law, which established the National Policy for Solidarity Economy and created the National System of Solidarity Economy (Sinaes) (Brasil, 2024). The law was named in honor of Paul Singer, who was described as one of the principal Brazilian scholars on the topic and who served as the head of the National Secretariat for Solidarity Economy in the first Lula government between 2003 and 2007 (Agência Senado, 2024). The Paul Singer Law defines solidarity economy enterprises as those with economic purposes but without profit-making as their end goal, self-managed by their members, and it stimulates associativism and cooperativism as characterizing features of these enterprises (Agência Brasil, 2024). The law also amended the Civil Code to include solidarity economy enterprises in the list of non-profit legal entities, giving them greater legal recognition and facilitating their formalization (Ministério Público do Paraná, 2025).

Regulation and Implementation

The Paul Singer Law was regulated by Decree No. 12.784 of December 19, 2025, which established the parameters for the National Policy for Solidarity Economy and created the National System for Solidarity Economy (Sinaes) (Brasil, 2025). The decree defines the policy as an instrument of state action with social participation and control, aimed at developing plans and actions to promote the solidarity economy. Its principles include non-discrimination and promotion of equal opportunities, generation of work and income through work organization focused on autonomy and self-management, articulation and integration of public policies for local and regional development, and stimulation of solidarity economy as a sustainable development strategy (Brasil, 2025). The decree also establishes guidelines for implementation, including participatory governance and social control, territorial action oriented toward integration and decentralization, intersectoral integration with social, environmental, economic, and human rights policies, and promotion of popular education and training processes in solidarity economy (Brasil, 2025).

The Fourth National Conference and Participatory Democracy

In August 2025, the Fourth National Conference on Popular and Solidarity Economy was held in Luziânia, Goiás, consolidating itself as a strategic space for evaluation and planning of popular and solidarity economy policy (Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, 2025). The conference brought together 985 elected delegates with representation from all states, diversity of gender and generation, and approximately 1,230 participants in total. The broad conferential process, which began in 2024, mobilized more than 16,000 people across 1,580 municipalities through 183 local conferences, 26 state conferences, one district conference, and 14 thematic and free conferences, demonstrating the policy's capillarity and the Ministry of Labor and Employment's capacity for territorial articulation (Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, 2025). The Final Report of the Fourth National Conference systematized the guidelines approved by the national plenary, consolidating 80 priority proposals that constitute the strategic reference guiding the elaboration of the Second National Plan for Popular and Solidarity Economy.

The National Registry of Solidarity Economic Enterprises

In 2025, the Ministry of Labor and Employment consolidated the restructuring of the National Registry of Solidarity Economic Enterprises (Cadsol), a registry created to promote public recognition of solidarity economy enterprises and enable their access to public policies (Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, 2025). One of the principal advances of the period was the updating of the ordinance establishing Cadsol through Ordinance MTE No. 481 of March 28, 2025. By the end of 2025, 2,600 solidarity economic enterprises were registered in the new version of Cadsol, which represents more than 130,000 associated people (Brasil, 2025). Throughout 2025, the State, Federal District, and Municipal Commissions and the National Commission for Registration and Information of Cadsol were reconstituted, with members from 28 commissions trained and qualified to analyze and deliberate on registration requests from solidarity economic enterprises. This decentralized validation process ensures that enterprise recognition occurs close to local realities (Ministério do Trabalho e Emprego, 2025).

Scale and Scope of the Solidarity Economy

The solidarity economy in Brazil encompasses a substantial number of enterprises and workers. According to data from the National Observatory of Solidarity Economy and Cooperativism, there are more than 19,000 solidarity economy enterprises spread throughout the country, involving more than 1.4 million workers in solidarity economy activities (Observatório Nacional da Economia Solidária e do Cooperativismo, 2025). In 2025, the federal government allocated 73.7 million reais to support solidarity economy initiatives, directly benefiting 639 enterprises (Brasil, 2025). The cooperative sector more broadly, which includes both solidarity economy enterprises and traditional cooperatives, reached 29 million cooperative members in 2025, equivalent to 13.6 percent of the Brazilian population, with cooperatives moving 848 billion reais in financial resources and generating 578,000 direct jobs (Somos Coop, 2026). These figures demonstrate that the solidarity economy, while still a minority of Brazil's overall economy, has achieved significant scale and institutional recognition.

Political Challenges and Structural Tensions

Despite important advances, the solidarity economy in Brazil faces significant political and structural challenges. A major report on platform cooperatives and digital solidarity economy during the Lula administration from 2023 to 2025 found that while the government developed pioneering initiatives, these advances coexist with the absence of public procurement mechanisms, dedicated credit lines, regulatory reform, and tax incentives (Soares Seto, 2026). Despite progress in the executive branch, platform cooperatives have faced judicial setbacks and legislative stagnation, with the current legal framework continuing to hinder their formalization and growth. The report notes that the public policy formulation process was highly participatory, involving academia and various social movements, but financing relied on discretionary funds, and official councils remained dominated by traditional cooperativism (Soares Seto, 2026). These tensions reveal a gap between the recognition of solidarity economy as a legitimate policy field and the concrete instruments needed to enable its expansion.

Access to Credit and Financial Constraints

Access to credit and financial services remains a persistent obstacle for solidarity economy enterprises in Brazil. Community banks face important challenges in terms of financing, as legislation prevents them from directly raising funds from the public, making these institutions dependent on public partnerships and support from universities and social organizations (Cofecon, n.d.). For recycling cooperatives, lack of working capital hinders collective commercialization of recyclables, while social exclusion and bureaucratic constraints prevent recyclers from obtaining official bank loans, perpetuating cycles of poverty, dependency, and exclusion (Oxfam Policy & Practice, 2026). The volume of financing available is still insufficient to meet the demands of solidarity enterprises, and access to credit, technical assistance, and public recognition of sustainable practices are identified as central challenges to be addressed in the coming years (Pepe Vargas, 2025, as cited in PT Assembleia RS). Some critics argue that solidarity economy will not flourish with "more of the same" in terms of capacity building, credit, and subsidies, because these tools, inherited from business promotion, reinforce competition rather than cooperation (Dagnino, 2025).

Gender, Race, and Intersectional Inequalities

The solidarity economy in Brazil, despite its emancipatory rhetoric, still reflects the structural inequalities of race, gender, class, and territoriality that characterize Brazilian society. Black women constitute the majority in solidarity economy enterprises, yet they face persistent barriers to accessing resources, decision-making spaces, and financial autonomy (Conceição, 2025). Women represent approximately 70 percent of the solidarity economy workforce in Brazil, and while they are present in management positions including presidencies and vice-presidencies, they remain underrepresented in financial direction and other strategic functions (Cofecon, n.d.). These challenges are especially acute in rural areas, where infrastructure is limited and access to public policies is more restricted (Conceição, 2025). The Justa Trama network, an emblematic example of solidarity economy organizing, brings together around 700 people, most of them women over the age of 40 with low levels of education, from six self-managed enterprises, demonstrating both the potential and the vulnerability of solidarity economy initiatives led by historically marginalized populations (Scielo, 2025).

The Digital Solidarity Economy and Platform Cooperativism

An emerging frontier for the solidarity economy in Brazil is the digital solidarity economy and platform cooperativism. The Brazilian government has developed pioneering initiatives in this area, including a public white-label platform designed for use by multiple cooperatives and the recognition of a new policy field called the Digital Solidarity Economy (Soares Seto, 2026). Federal investment reached 2.6 million dollars directed to the development of two platforms built in partnership with public universities for driver and delivery cooperatives, introducing fundamental innovations in data governance and the design of algorithmic systems under worker control (Soares Seto, 2026). However, the report notes that building a viable ecosystem requires coordinated action across financing, technology infrastructure, governance, training, legislation, and movement building that extends beyond electoral cycles. The digital solidarity economy represents both an opportunity to extend cooperative principles to the digital realm and a challenge to the dominance of large technology corporations in platform capitalism.

Solidarity Economy During and After the COVID-19 Pandemic

The COVID-19 pandemic, which affected Brazil severely beginning in March 2020, posed significant challenges for solidarity economy enterprises while also demonstrating their resilience and capacity for adaptation. New hygiene requirements caused difficulties for farmers' markets and other collective commercialization arrangements, leading solidarity economy networks to restructure or relocate markets, establish online ordering systems, engage with solidarity delivery systems, and supply vulnerable individuals as solidarity actions (FAO, 2026). Monetary transfers through social currencies, created to mitigate the effects of the pandemic while managing local policies, reflected the values and institutional dynamics shaped by local politics, including conservatism and the contradictions inherent in Brazil's experience with cash transfers (Scielo Costa Rica, n.d.). Research on solidarity economy enterprises in the municipality of Araraquara examined the impacts of the pandemic on the life of solidarity economy groups, identifying processes of creation, mortality, strengthening, and weakening of enterprises during this period (Periodicos UFPB, 2025). The pandemic experience highlighted both the vulnerabilities of solidarity economy enterprises to external shocks and their capacity for mutual support and collective adaptation.

Critical Perspectives and Future Directions

The solidarity economy in Brazil faces ongoing criticism regarding its effectiveness and its relationship to the broader economic system. Specialists point out that despite good intentions, many solidarity economy initiatives face difficulties in fitting into the real economy. Cooperatives, for example, often do not operate in a truly egalitarian manner, as they may replicate hierarchical structures present in other organizational models (Jornal USP, 2025). Challenges such as commercial strategies, ideological preservation, access to credit, and technical capacitation have been identified as interconnected to the realization of solidarity economy ideals, highlighting the need for favorable measures to overcome these obstacles (UNIFESP, n.d.). The fourth national conference approved 80 proposals to strengthen popular solidarity economy, and since 2023 the conference process has reestablished 100 national councils and resumed 28 conferences held across the country with the objective of listening to the population (Agência Brasil, 2025). The future of the solidarity economy in Brazil will depend on its ability to navigate political cycles, secure stable financing, address internal inequalities, and demonstrate its viability as a scalable alternative to conventional economic models.

Conclusion

The social economy and solidarity economy in Brazil represent a dynamic and evolving field that has achieved significant institutional recognition while facing persistent structural challenges. From its emergence in the 1980s as a response to neoliberal restructuring to the recent approval of the Paul Singer Law and the holding of the Fourth National Conference, the movement has demonstrated a capacity for organization, advocacy, and policy innovation. The creation of SENAES in 2003, its dismantling in 2019, and its reinstatement in 2023 illustrate the political volatility that characterizes the sector's institutional environment. The challenges of access to credit, gender and racial inequality, legal recognition of platform cooperatives, and the need for stable financing mechanisms remain central to the agenda of solidarity economy actors and policymakers. With more than 19,000 enterprises and 1.4 million workers involved, and with the cooperative sector more broadly reaching 29 million members, the solidarity economy in Brazil constitutes a significant social and economic force that continues to shape debates about alternative models of development in the country.

Introduction

The social and solidarity economy in Ecuador represents a distinctive model of economic organization that places human well-being and community cooperation above purely profit-driven motives. Known locally as the Economía Popular y Solidaria (EPS), this sector has deep historical roots in the country's ancestral traditions and has evolved into a legally recognized pillar of the national economy. Ecuador stands out in Latin America for its constitutional recognition of this economic model, which has shaped public policy and financial inclusion strategies over the past two decades (Ruiz-Rivera & Lemaître, 2019). Understanding the social economy in Ecuador requires examining its historical foundations, its legal institutionalization, and the contemporary political debates that shape its future.

Historical Background

The origins of solidarity-based economic practices in Ecuador stretch back well before the Spanish conquest. Indigenous communities in the Andean region organized production around principles of reciprocity, communal labor, and the philosophy of Suma Kawsay, which emphasizes living in harmony with nature and community (Castro Carpio et al., 2022). These ancestral forms of economic organization prioritized collective benefit over individual accumulation, establishing a cultural foundation that would later inform modern solidarity economy movements. The cooperative tradition began to formalize in the nineteenth century when ideas of mutual aid and cooperation arrived from Western Europe, leading to the emergence of mutualist associations and early cooperatives (Ruiz-Rivera & Lemaître, 2019). The first documented cooperative experience in Ecuador dates to 1822, linked to General Bartolomé Salom, marking the beginning of an institutional trajectory that would gradually expand throughout the following century (Vicepresidencia de la República, n.d.).

The Cooperative and Associative Movement

The twentieth century witnessed significant growth in cooperative and associative organizations across Ecuador. During the 1960s and 1970s, a self-management movement emerged that sought to differentiate itself from both market capitalism and state-controlled economies (Secretaría Nacional de Planificación, 2022). These organizations reflected a critical perspective on conventional economic models and aimed to create alternatives that prioritized community welfare. The cooperative movement expanded particularly in rural areas, where savings and credit cooperatives became vital sources of financing for small producers and families excluded from traditional banking systems. By the late twentieth century, the concept of "solidarity economy" had spread across South America through international academic networks, influencing how Ecuadorian organizations understood and articulated their economic practices (Ruiz-Rivera & Lemaître, 2019). This period marked a transition from isolated cooperative efforts to a more cohesive social movement with a shared identity and political agenda.

Constitutional Recognition and Legal Framework

A turning point for the social and solidarity economy in Ecuador came with the 2008 Constitution, which officially recognized the popular and solidarity economy as one of the pillars of the country's economic system. Article 283 of the Constitution establishes that the economic system is social and solidarity-based, recognizing the human being as both subject and purpose, and seeking a dynamic and balanced relationship between society, the state, and the market in harmony with nature (Asamblea Nacional del Ecuador, 2008, as cited in Secretaría Nacional de Planificación, 2022). This constitutional framework was reinforced by the Organic Law of the Popular and Solidarity Economy and the Popular and Solidarity Financial System, enacted in 2011, which regulates and promotes organizational forms based on solidarity, cooperation, and self-management (Global Social Economy Forum, 2025). The law created the Superintendence of Popular and Solidarity Economy (SEPS) as a specialized regulatory body, demonstrating Ecuador's commitment to institutionalizing this economic model in a way that is unique in the region (Cajamarca Simbaña et al., 2025).

The Financial Dimension

The popular and solidarity financial sector has experienced remarkable growth since the constitutional reform. Credit cooperatives and mutualist institutions have become essential vehicles for financing economic activity, particularly for segments of the population that traditional banks have historically underserved. According to the SEPS 2023 Accountability Report, the solidarity financial sector comprised 489 savings and credit cooperatives, one mutualist, and one central bank, with total assets reaching approximately $20 billion and a credit portfolio of $15 billion (Cajamarca Simbaña et al., 2025). The loan portfolio of these institutions grew from $2 billion at the end of 2010 to $20 billion in mid-2025, increasing their share of credit to the private sector from under 15 percent in the early 2010s to nearly 30 percent by 2025 (Cairn.info, 2026). This expansion has contributed significantly to financial inclusion, which rose from 37 percent in the early 2010s to nearly 65 percent at the end of 2024, supporting economic development and poverty reduction.

Economic Contribution and Employment

The social and solidarity economy plays a substantial role in Ecuador's overall economic landscape. The sector encompasses approximately 65 percent of active productive units in the country and generates more than 1.2 million direct and indirect jobs (Cajamarca Simbaña et al., 2025). Popular and solidarity economy organizations number around 5,280 throughout Ecuador, with the participation of 153,390 registered members (Food and Agriculture Organization, n.d.). Despite these impressive figures, only about 1.02 percent of these organizations are community-based enterprises operating in food production and processing, suggesting significant potential for further development in this area. The sector's contribution extends beyond employment generation to include the strengthening of local economic circuits, the promotion of fair trade practices, and the preservation of traditional productive activities that might otherwise disappear under competitive market pressures.

Political Issues and Challenges

Despite its constitutional recognition and institutional framework, the social and solidarity economy in Ecuador faces several significant political and structural challenges. One recurring issue concerns the tension between the transformative discourse of the solidarity economy and the practical implementation of public policies. Research reveals systematic tensions between substantive policy discourse and formal implementation practices, creating what scholars describe as an institutionalization paradox where policies designed to support alternative economic models inadvertently reproduce the market rationalities they seek to transcend (EconPapers, 2026). Public procurement, for instance, has been identified as a strategic ally for the social economy, yet organizations face significant barriers when attempting to participate in these processes, including complex requirements and limited capacity (Scielo, 2026). These implementation gaps limit the sector's ability to fully realize its potential as an alternative development model.

Organizational Weaknesses and Structural Limitations

The popular and solidarity economy sector also contends with internal structural weaknesses that constrain its consolidation and sustainability. Many organizations face organizational fragmentation, limited horizontal cooperation, and a lack of coordination among actors within the sector (EBSCO, 2026). A significant limiting factor is the low level of higher education among entrepreneurs in the sector, particularly in financial and accounting matters, which restricts their capacity for effective decision-making, innovation, and adoption of emerging technologies (Zenodo, 2026). Survey research conducted in Guaranda found that while 85 percent of entrepreneurs had heard of the solidarity economy law, participation in training and workshops remained notably low, with most engagement occurring through meetings and fairs rather than structured capacity-building activities (Zenodo, 2026). These educational and organizational gaps represent obstacles to the sector's professionalization and long-term viability.

Current Political Context and Social Tensions

The broader political context in Ecuador has presented both opportunities and challenges for the social and solidarity economy in recent years. The government of President Daniel Noboa has taken steps to support the sector, including the delivery of $62 million to popular and solidarity economy sectors between November 2025 and January 2026, and the provision of $7.1 million in non-reimbursable resources to organizations and communities of Indigenous, Afro-Ecuadorian, and Montubio peoples for productive subprojects (Secretaría General de Comunicación, 2026). However, the country simultaneously faces severe security, socioeconomic, and environmental challenges that affect the entire economy. Violence driven by drug-related crime has escalated sharply, making Ecuador one of the most insecure countries in the region, while poverty remains high at 21.4 percent and extreme poverty at 8.3 percent (World Food Programme, 2026). Government austerity measures, including the removal of fuel subsidies and increases in value-added tax, have triggered social tensions and nationwide protests, creating an uncertain environment for solidarity economy organizations that depend on stable public support.

Institutional Support and Public Policy

The Ecuadorian state has developed various mechanisms to promote and strengthen the social and solidarity economy. The Institute of Popular and Solidarity Economy (IEPS) leads initiatives such as the Project for the Strengthening of Community Economies in the Territories of Indigenous, Afro-Ecuadorian, and Montubio Peoples, implemented with support from the World Bank (Secretaría General de Comunicación, 2026). The National Corporation for Popular and Solidarity Finance (CONAFIPS) channels credit to cooperatives and associations, with $23 million directed toward the cooperative sector to stimulate production and employment (Expreso, 2026). Despite these efforts, stakeholders have called for urgent reform of the Organic Law of Popular and Solidarity Economy, which has been in force for 14 years, to allow organizations to compete more effectively under current economic conditions (Instituto de Economía Popular y Solidaria, n.d.). The need to update the legal framework reflects the evolving nature of the sector and the challenges it faces in adapting to contemporary economic realities.

The Role of Local Governments and Community Networks

Decentralized autonomous governments play a fundamental role in supporting the social and solidarity economy at the local level. These governments contribute to productive development by supporting small-scale producers through training and by providing marketing spaces such as fairs and markets, which reinforce the engagement of local communities in collaborative economic development (Global Social Economy Forum, 2025). Producer organizations have joined together in networks to work collaboratively and pool their productive resources, with some operating at the local level while others achieve national influence. These networks enable producers to collaborate, share knowledge, and access training opportunities, strengthening their production capacity to access better market opportunities. The experience of Salinas de Guaranda, a village that has developed since the 1970s around a solidarity and community economy model, illustrates how a network of cooperatives can transform local economies and improve living conditions (Dumas, 2017).

Community Economies and Indigenous Peoples

An important dimension of Ecuador's social economy concerns the distinction between the popular and solidarity economy and the community economies of Indigenous peoples and nationalities. While these concepts are often conflated, they are not necessarily equivalent. Community economies are rooted in the family and community as fundamental units, governed by principles that have persisted through centuries of external pressures (Ministerio de Gobierno, 2021). The interaction between community economies and other economic forms, including the popular and solidarity economy, has led to transformations in their principles and practices, yet these economies continue to represent coherent expressions of a worldview centered on the maintenance and reproduction of life. Recognizing this distinction is essential for designing public policies that respect the autonomy and specific characteristics of Indigenous and Afro-Ecuadorian economic practices while promoting their integration into broader solidarity economy networks.

Conclusion

The social and solidarity economy in Ecuador represents both a historical continuity of ancestral practices and a modern institutional innovation. Its constitutional recognition in 2008 and the subsequent legal framework established the country as a regional leader in recognizing alternative economic models. The sector's financial dimension has grown impressively, with credit cooperatives now accounting for nearly 30 percent of private sector credit and contributing to significant improvements in financial inclusion. However, the solidarity economy confronts persistent challenges, including implementation gaps in public policy, organizational weaknesses, educational limitations among entrepreneurs, and a broader political context marked by security concerns and fiscal constraints. The future of the sector will depend on the ability of policymakers, organizations, and communities to address these challenges while preserving the principles of solidarity, cooperation, and harmony with nature that define this distinctive economic model. As Ecuador navigates uncertain political and economic waters, the social and solidarity economy remains a vital space for constructing more inclusive and sustainable forms of economic life.

name: South Africa
title: The State of the Social Economy and Solidarity in South Africa
summary: The social and solidarity economy in South Africa represents a distinct approach to economic organisation that prioritises collective benefit, democratic participation, and social purpose over unrestricted profit. article:
Introduction

The social and solidarity economy in South Africa represents a distinct approach to economic organisation that prioritises collective benefit, democratic participation, and social purpose over unrestricted profit. Deputy Minister Mmapaseka Steve Letsike has described cooperatives, mutual organisations, associations, community enterprises, and qualifying social-purpose businesses as organisations that undertake real economic activity while placing collective benefit ahead of private gain (Letsike, 2026). This economic model has deep roots in African traditions of reciprocal labour, rotating savings, mutual aid, and communal stewardship, values expressed through the philosophy of Ubuntu, which reminds us that personhood is formed through relationship and that individual wellbeing is inseparable from the well-being of others (Letsike, 2026).

Historical Background

The historical foundations of South Africa's social economy stretch back long before the term entered policy documents. African societies practised mutual aid and collective responsibility across the continent, and colonialism reorganised these economies around dispossession, extraction, and migrant labour, while apartheid deepened that architecture by separating people from land and preventing the majority from accumulating productive power (Letsike, 2026). The scholarly literature on South Africa's democratic transition generally recognises the decisive role of organised labour and black trade union organisations in the collapse of the apartheid regime, with labour's social citizenship discourse positioning wage labour as a vehicle of social inclusion and collective solidarity (Satgar, 2024). Following the first democratic elections in 1994, the African National Congress government proclaimed a commitment to cooperative development through its Reconstruction and Development Programme, and in 2005 a new Cooperatives Act was passed after five years of refinement with input from government, the cooperative movement, and independent support organisations (United Nations, 2015).

The Emergence of the Solidarity Economy

The emergence of the solidarity economy in South Africa was facilitated by three important conditions: the end of institutionalised and regulated apartheid, the crisis of South Africa's neoliberalised political economy, and grassroots anti-capitalist emancipatory organising (Satgar, 2024). The solidarity economy alternative is rooted in South African left thought and has been evolving its own theoretical framework while learning from international experiences as it engages in grassroots practice. It is an emancipatory and anti-capitalist grassroots alternative that seeks exits, departure points, escapes, and breakthroughs beyond the ecocidal logic of contemporary capitalism to sustain life (Satgar, 2024). The Cooperative and Policy Alternative Centre and the various social forces it works with have embraced an open-ended notion of the solidarity economy as a collective humanist response and democratic alternative from below to the crisis we face, drawing on common humanity as the basis for solidarity action (Satgar, 2024).

Political Issues and Challenges

The political landscape surrounding the social and solidarity economy in South Africa is marked by significant tensions and unresolved questions. Letsike (2026) linked the development of an inclusive economy to South Africa's history of colonialism and apartheid, arguing that dispossession, extraction, migrant labour, and exclusion from productive assets had left a legacy that continued to shape economic inequality. The persistence of unemployment, poverty, inequality, and spatial exclusion makes the urgency of constitutional implementation even clearer, she said. However, the social and solidarity economy faces the risk of becoming another name for poverty or informal economic activity. Letsike (2026) cautioned that it cannot become cheap outsourcing of public responsibilities, nor can social purpose excuse poor governance or exploitation.

Policy Framework and Institutional Support

South Africa's approach to promoting sustained economic growth and decent work is firmly anchored in the Constitution, with commitments operationalised through the National Development Plan Vision 2030 and the Medium Term Development Plan 2024-2029, which emphasise inclusive growth, job creation, and productivity improvements (Statistics South Africa, n.d.). A draft Social and Solidarity Economy policy was developed with the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition, and the International Labour Organization has been working with South African stakeholders to promote the social and solidarity economy to tackle entrenched challenges of inequality, unemployment, and poverty (ILO, 2025). The ILO co-hosted a groundbreaking roundtable in November 2024 that reignited conversations on the crucial importance of the social and solidarity economy in South Africa, building on numerous ILO projects from 2010 to 2021 (ILO, 2025).

Economic Context and Employment Challenges

The need for a stronger social and solidarity economy sector is particularly urgent given South Africa's severe employment challenges. Deputy Minister Letsike cited economic growth of 0.5% in the first quarter of 2026, but noted that growth had not translated into inclusion at the scale required, with 8.5 million South Africans officially unemployed in the second quarter and an unemployment rate of 33.6% (Letsike, 2026). Youth unemployment had risen to 47.4%, while the unemployment rate for women stood at 37.5%, more than seven percentage points higher than that of men. Government programmes such as the Presidential Employment Stimulus and Social Employment Fund have created important entry points into the world of work, generating more than 2.5 million work and livelihood opportunities, mainly for young people and women, but the next challenge is to ensure that temporary opportunities become bridges to accredited skills, permanent employment, cooperative ownership, community enterprises, and sustainable contracts (Letsike, 2026).

Access to Finance and the Missing Middle

Access to finance remains one of the most significant barriers facing social enterprises and cooperatives in South Africa (Department of Employment and Labour, n.d.). The so-called missing middle has been highlighted as a major obstacle facing community enterprises and cooperatives, referring not only to the gap between micro-grants and commercial lending but also to broader difficulties accessing appropriate finance, markets, contracts, and institutional support (Letsike, 2026). Women-led community enterprises may have demand and experience but lack collateral, audited financial statements, or the capacity to compete for large tenders. A recent assessment identified 117 public MSME-financing mechanisms administered by 26 institutions, suggesting that the challenge is not necessarily a lack of resources but rather a problem of coordination and accessibility (Letsike, 2026). Research has shown that institutional voids in the Integrated Development Plan, stemming from the constrained development focus of municipalities, manifest in deficient sector engagement and deficient accountability for social entrepreneurship (Tshikovhi & Shambare, 2024).

The Double Burden of Compliance

Social entrepreneurs in South Africa face what has been described as a double burden of compliance and the need to streamline processes to unlock the potential of the social and solidarity economy. One attendee at an ILO roundtable remarked that running a social enterprise in South Africa means first registering a PTY and then an NPO, which involves too much red tape and compliance requirements (ILO, 2025). This regulatory complexity creates significant obstacles for small-scale social economy organisations, particularly those operating in marginalised communities where administrative capacity is limited. The regulatory environment also fails to adequately recognise the distinctive character of social economy organisations, treating them either as conventional for-profit businesses or as non-profit entities, rather than acknowledging their hybrid nature.

Cooperative Development and Grassroots Practice

Cooperatives are recognised as a backbone of many economies across the globe, and in South Africa they are the heart of the much-needed village and township economic revival (National Development Agency, 2025). The South African Federation of Trade Unions has publicly called for community mining cooperatives as part of nationalisation to support small-scale informal miners (Satgar, 2024). In early 2018, Oxfam South Africa hosted a workshop that contributed to the development of solidarity economy movements' webpage for grassroots-driven cooperatives. More recently, the United Communities Consumer Co-operative has been established as a secondary cooperative linking local consumer cooperatives into one national movement of ownership, participation, and solidarity, described as a people's economy grounded in ownership, co-operation, self-reliance, and solidarity (South African Communist Party, 2025). StreetNet and WIEGO have jointly launched the first ever social and solidarity economy toolkit aimed specifically at street and market vendors, recognising that savings and credit groups are the main way that street and market vendors can organise their first social and solidarity economy unit (StreetNet International, 2025).

Social Protection and Worker Rights

Many informal, cooperative, platform, and community-based workers face risks associated with illness, injury, and loss of income, yet may not enjoy the same protections as workers in formal employment (Department of Employment and Labour, n.d.). This gap in social protection represents a significant challenge for the social and solidarity economy, as it means that workers in these alternative economic forms remain vulnerable to economic shocks and health emergencies without adequate safety nets. Addressing this disparity requires policy interventions that extend social protection coverage to workers in the social and solidarity economy, recognising the distinctive nature of their employment relationships and the collective forms of organisation that characterise their work.

The State and Democratic Systemic Reform

The relationship between the solidarity economy and the South African state is complex and evolving. The notion of democratic systemic reform captures how solidarity economy agentic forces think about and approach the role of the state, seeking to bring together democratic grassroots power, deep system transformation, and embedded state reform into the process of building solidarity economy logics (Satgar, 2024). However, solidarity economy forces have also critiqued and distanced themselves from some practices of the South African state, particularly the state's hybridising of nationalism with discursive elements that skew cooperative development in the direction of market-centred accumulation, failed financing approaches, and top-down movement building (Satgar, 2024). This critical engagement reflects the solidarity economy's commitment to grassroots agency and its resistance to co-optation by state-centric developmentalism or market fundamentalism.

International Perspectives and Global Momentum

The global momentum behind the social and solidarity economy has been building, with a recent United Nations resolution on the subject and growing recognition of its critical role in addressing poverty, inequality, and decent work (ILO, 2025). ILO Director Alexio Musindo highlighted this momentum and underscored the ILO's commitment to promoting decent work and social justice, which aligns with social and solidarity economy principles. He called for collective responsibility to leverage this momentum, especially as South Africa prepares to assume the G20 Presidency under the theme of Solidarity, Equality, and Sustainable Development (ILO, 2025). International examples, such as Italy's social cooperatives that share services and bid collectively, offer models that South Africa could adapt to its own context. The Deputy Minister called for every district to map its cooperatives, mutuals, and community enterprises together with local needs, suggesting a bottom-up approach to developing the sector (Letsike, 2026).

Conclusion

The state of the social economy and solidarity in South Africa presents a picture of significant potential constrained by persistent structural challenges. The sector draws on deep-rooted African traditions of mutual aid and collective responsibility, yet operates within an economic system shaped by colonial and apartheid legacies of dispossession and exclusion. While policy frameworks and government programmes have created important entry points, access to finance, regulatory complexity, and the absence of adequate social protection for workers in alternative economic forms remain major obstacles. The social and solidarity economy offers a genuine alternative to both state-centric developmentalism and market fundamentalism, one that places democratic participation, collective ownership, and social purpose at the centre of economic life. Realising this potential will require not only policy reform but also a fundamental shift in how economic value and success are understood and measured in South African society.

name: Uruguay
title: The State of the Social Economy and Solidarity in Uruguay
summary: Uruguay has one of the longest and most deeply rooted traditions of social economy and solidarity in Latin America. article:
Historical Background

Uruguay has one of the longest and most deeply rooted traditions of social economy and solidarity in Latin America. The origins of this movement can be traced back to the mid-nineteenth century, when waves of European immigrants arrived in the country and brought with them ideas of mutual aid and cooperative organization. The first mutual aid society was founded in 1853 by Spanish residents in Montevideo, and by 1870 a group of printing workers had established a mutual support organization. The first consumer cooperative is recognized as having been founded in 1889 in the Old City of Montevideo (Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History, 2025). These early experiences were not isolated experiments. They were part of a broader social response to the limited presence of the state in providing protection and services for working people. Mutualism and cooperativism developed in dialogue with the distinct stages of Uruguayan history and became a defining feature of the country's social fabric (Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History, 2025).

The Growth of Cooperativism

Throughout the twentieth century, cooperativism expanded into many sectors of the Uruguayan economy. Housing cooperatives became particularly important. Under the system known as mutual aid, groups of families contributed their own labor to build their homes collectively, combining state subsidies with their own work (Global Pact Colombia, n.d.). This model allowed nearly sixty percent of Uruguayans to own a dignified home, including people with limited economic resources. Today, cooperatives and rural development societies generate more than 29,000 jobs, representing about 2.2 percent of national employment (Office of Planning and Budget, n.d.). The sector has experienced significant growth over the past fifteen years, with the number of cooperative experiences tripling during that period (Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History, 2025).

Legal and Institutional Framework

A major step forward came in 2009 with the approval of Law No. 18,407 on cooperatives and the cooperative system. This law provided a comprehensive legal framework for the sector. A decade later, in December 2019, the Uruguayan Senate approved Law No. 19,848, which declared the promotion, dissemination, stimulation, and development of the social and solidarity economy to be of national interest (International Labour Organization, 2020). This law established a definition of the social and solidarity economy and provided a regulatory and promotional policy framework for the sector (Parlamento UY, 2026). The law aims to recognize, promote, and support private entities that prioritize people and the common interest over capital, based on solidarity, cooperation, and democratic management (Parlamento UY, 2026). In April 2026, the National Institute of Cooperativism (INACOOP) constituted the first Consultative Council of the Social and Solidarity Economy, a body made up of seventeen public and private organizations (INACOOP, 2026).

The FONDES Experience and Its Controversies

The creation of the Fund for Development (FONDES) in 2015 marked another important moment for the social economy in Uruguay. Law No. 19,337 established this fund to provide financing for cooperatives, self-managed enterprises, and recovered companies. A portion of the fund, known as FONDES-INACOOP, was specifically oriented toward cooperativism, self-management, and the solidarity economy (INACOOP, n.d.). However, the FONDES became a subject of intense political debate. Critics argued that the fund lacked proper oversight and that some resources were used without meeting legal requirements (Parlamento UY, n.d.). The opposition criticized the mechanism as poorly designed and rushed. These controversies reflected broader tensions within the governing Broad Front coalition itself regarding the orientation of the fund. Some sectors wanted to focus on small and medium enterprises through the National Development Agency, while others defended the self-managed and transformative character of the social economy (INACOOP, n.d.).

The Role of Mutualism in Health Care

Mutualism has played a particularly important role in Uruguay's health care system. Mutual aid institutions, known as mutualistas, emerged in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries as organized social responses to the need for health coverage in a context of strong European immigration and limited state intervention (Observatory of Health, 2026). These institutions were created by communities of immigrants who used different philosophical approaches, ranging from anarchist to Catholic, to shape their organizations (Library of Congress, n.d.). Over time, mutualistas became specialized as health service providers and were categorized as Collective Medical Assistance Institutions. Today, they remain a cornerstone of Uruguay's health system, providing medical assistance to hundreds of thousands of members without pursuing profit (International Labour Organization, n.d.).

Social Economy and Public Policies

The arrival of the Broad Front in government in 2005 opened new spaces for state recognition of the social economy. Public policies for the promotion and support of the sector were strengthened, leading to the tripling of cooperative experiences over the following fifteen years (Oxford Research Encyclopedia of Latin American History, 2025). The government promoted cooperativism to respond to various public problems, including social inclusion through work. The Ministry of Social Development implemented a program of social cooperatives between 2005 and 2019 to provide employment opportunities for vulnerable populations (Sistema de Información Científica, n.d.). In 2026, a training and capacity-building program for cooperatives received approximately 75 million pesos to strengthen the cooperative system and the social and solidarity economy, with execution planned for 2026 and 2027 (Government of Uruguay, 2026).

Current Challenges: Child Poverty and Inequality

Despite its robust social protection system and one of the highest levels of social spending in Latin America, Uruguay faces significant challenges. Around 320,000 children and adolescents are growing up in conditions of deprivation, according to UNICEF (World Bank, 2025). Four out of every ten children in Uruguayan households face monetary poverty, multidimensional poverty, or both simultaneously. Public spending per child is less than half that for adults over sixty, and the monetary poverty rate among children is five times higher than among older adults. The poverty rate among children under six was 29.1 percent in 2025, more than twelve percentage points above the national average (Debate, 2026). These figures highlight a structural imbalance in Uruguay's social contract, which has been remarkably successful in reducing poverty among older adults but has not achieved the same results for children.

Political Debates and Policy Proposals

The social economy and solidarity sector is not immune to political tensions. In recent years, the PIT-CNT labor federation has proposed applying a one percent tax on the wealth of the country's richest citizens to dedicate those resources to combating child poverty (Prensa Latina, 2025). This proposal has been supported by some sectors of the Broad Front but has generated debate within the coalition. The government has also faced criticism for the slow pace of change in areas such as public safety, child poverty, and social security (Bertelsmann Stiftung, 2026). Trade unions have noted progress in transparency, poverty reduction, job creation, and human development, but they also point to persistent challenges in child poverty, informality, the gender wage gap, and disparities between territories (International Trade Union Confederation, n.d.).

Statistics and Reach of the Sector

The social economy in Uruguay is substantial in scale. According to recent data, the sector includes more than one million members and approximately 1,813 cooperatives (Revistas UVigo, 2024). In 2023, social cooperatives generated 4,426 jobs, an increase of 7.9 percent compared to the previous year (INACOOP, 2024). Cooperatives and social economy organizations sustain approximately 30,000 jobs throughout the country (INACOOP, 2026). The housing cooperative model has been particularly successful, with more than 20,000 homes built through a system that combines state subsidies and the collective labor of cooperative members (Global Pact Colombia, n.d.). These numbers demonstrate that the social economy is not a marginal phenomenon in Uruguay but a significant component of the national economy and social fabric.

International Recognition and Cooperation

Uruguay's experience with the social economy has received international recognition. In 2022, the International Labour Organization reaffirmed Recommendation 193, which establishes that the promotion of cooperatives is a key international instrument to guide governments in creating favorable environments for cooperativism (INACOOP, 2026). In 2023, the United Nations emphasized that the social and solidarity economy contributes to inclusive and sustainable economic growth, fostering a new balance between economic, social, and environmental efficiency (Parlamento UY, 2026). Uruguay has also participated in regional initiatives such as the Mercosur Structural Convergence Fund, which is based on the principle of solidarity among member states (Government of Uruguay, 2024). These international frameworks provide important support for the continued development of the sector.

The Consultative Council and Future Directions

The creation of the Consultative Council of the Social and Solidarity Economy in 2026 represents a significant institutional development. This council is a consultative body of INACOOP whose objective is to propose policies, strategies, plans, and programs for the promotion and strengthening of the social and solidarity economy (INACOOP, 2026). The council includes seventeen organizations and serves as a space for discussion and elaboration of proposals for the sector as a whole. One of its first initiatives was to establish an agreement with the Legislative Branch so that social economy organizations can provide services and supplies to the Parliament through a competitive purchasing system (Parlamento UY, 2026). This initiative aims to favor the insertion and development of social economy enterprises as suppliers of the state, creating new opportunities for the sector.

Conclusion

The social economy and solidarity in Uruguay represent a rich and complex reality. From the mutual aid societies of the nineteenth century to the legal framework of the twenty-first century, the sector has evolved and adapted to the changing needs of Uruguayan society. Cooperativism, mutualism, and self-management have become integral parts of the country's social and economic landscape. The sector generates employment, provides housing, offers health care, and contributes to social inclusion. At the same time, significant challenges remain, particularly in addressing child poverty and reducing inequalities. The political debates surrounding the social economy reflect broader questions about the role of the state, the distribution of resources, and the meaning of solidarity in contemporary Uruguay. The future of the sector will depend on the ability of political actors, social organizations, and citizens to continue building on this tradition while addressing the persistent challenges that remain.

name: Canada
title: The State of the Social Economy and Solidarity in Canada
summary: The social economy in Canada refers to a broad sector of organizations that use business strategies to achieve social, cultural, and environmental goals. These organizations are not driven primarily by profit for private shareholders. Instead, they reinvest surpluses to serve their members and...
article:
Defining the Social Economy

The social economy in Canada refers to a broad sector of organizations that use business strategies to achieve social, cultural, and environmental goals. These organizations are not driven primarily by profit for private shareholders. Instead, they reinvest surpluses to serve their members and communities. Human Resources and Skills Development Canada has described the social economy as a grass-roots entrepreneurial, not-for-profit sector based on democratic values that seeks to enhance social, economic, and environmental conditions, often with a focus on disadvantaged members (HRSDC, 2005, as cited in Statistics Canada, 2010). The sector includes cooperatives, credit unions, non-profit organizations, charities, mutual societies, and emerging social enterprises. In Quebec, the legal definition is more precise. The Social Economy Act of 2013 states that social economy enterprises are operated according to principles including a purpose to meet the needs of members or the community, democratic governance, and the primacy of persons over capital (Social Economy Act, 2013).

Historical Background

The roots of Canada's social economy stretch back to the nineteenth century. The cooperative movement took hold in the late 1800s and early 1900s, with farmers forming grain cooperatives and communities establishing credit unions to access fair financial services. The Antigonish Movement in Nova Scotia during the 1920s and 1930s promoted cooperative enterprises as a path out of poverty for fishing and farming communities. However, the modern social economy as a recognized policy field emerged much later. In Quebec, a critical moment came in 1995 with the Women's March Against Poverty. Women marched from Montreal to Quebec City to demand greater investment in social services and housing. This movement, combined with the strength of community and cooperative networks, pushed the provincial government to embrace the social economy as a tool for job creation and social development (ILO, 2022). A conference on the social and economic future of Quebec in 1996 led to the creation of a working group on the social economy, and the approach of multi-stakeholder dialogue became a defining feature of the Quebec model (ILO, 2022).

The Quebec Model as a Pioneer

Quebec stands out as the most developed social economy ecosystem in Canada. The province passed the Social Economy Act in 2013, the first of its kind in Canada. This law recognizes the social economy's contribution to socioeconomic development and requires the government to adopt action plans to support it (Social Economy Act, 2013). The most recent plan, the fourth Government Action Plan in Social Economy for 2025 to 2030, was announced in July 2025. It prioritizes strategic sectors including housing, elder care, and environmental preservation. The Chantier de l'économie sociale, a non-partisan organization founded in 1999, serves as a hub for promoting and developing collective entrepreneurship in the province. It brings together cooperatives and non-profit organizations across many sectors (Chantier de l'économie sociale, 2025). Quebec's social economy comprises approximately 11,200 businesses, generates nearly $48 billion in sales, and employs over 220,000 people. Women make up 64 percent of this workforce (ILO, 2022).

The Social Economy Outside Quebec

Outside Quebec, the social economy has developed more slowly and unevenly. The OECD has classified Canada outside Quebec as having an emerging social economy, in contrast to Quebec's established model (Mendell, 2005). The federal government showed significant interest in the social economy around 2004. That year's federal budget allocated $132 million for capacity building, financing, and research. The government also committed to making social enterprises eligible for programs available to small businesses (Social Development Canada, 2005). A major research initiative, the Canadian Social Economy Research Partnerships, was funded by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. This program connected researchers and practitioners across the country and led to the creation of the Canadian Social Economy Hub. The Canadian Community Economic Development Network, known as CCEDNet, has been a key national voice for the sector. CCEDNet is a member of the global movement RIPESS, which promotes the social and solidarity economy as a vehicle to transform poverty and inequality (CCEDNet, 2009).

The Rise of Social Enterprise

Social enterprise has become an increasingly prominent part of the social economy in Canada. Social enterprises are businesses that trade goods or services in the market but redirect their surpluses toward social and community goals. They operate in diverse fields including employment training, food services, retail, and community health. A recent national snapshot found that over 400 social enterprises across Canada generated more than $6.5 billion in revenue in 2025. These enterprises employed 18,000 people, including over 5,600 individuals facing barriers to traditional employment. Twenty-two percent launched a new service or enterprise in the previous year (Buy Social Canada, 2026). This data reveals a sector with significant economic weight and a clear social mission. However, social enterprises face persistent challenges in accessing finance and public procurement opportunities, which limits their potential for growth (Buy Social Canada, 2026).

Social Finance and Impact Investing

The growth of social finance has introduced new tools and debates to Canada's social economy. Social impact bonds are one such instrument. These are pay-for-success arrangements where private investors provide upfront capital for social programs, and governments repay the investment only if predetermined outcomes are achieved. Since 2014, Canada has launched four social impact bonds (School of Public Policy, 2026). The federal government identified social finance and social innovation as priorities in 2015. Some supporters argue that social impact bonds can mobilize private capital for proven social innovations that governments have been reluctant to fund. Critics, however, warn that these instruments can prioritize measurable outcomes over holistic community needs and may expose social programs to the volatility of financial markets. The federal government has also supported the Investment Readiness Program to help social enterprises develop the capacity to access investment capital. CCEDNet serves as a convenor of program partners in this area (CCEDNet, 2023).

The Social Economy and Indigenous Communities

The relationship between the social economy and Indigenous communities in Canada is complex and requires careful attention. Indigenous peoples have long practiced forms of economic organization rooted in reciprocity, collective ownership, and community well-being. These traditions align in some ways with social economy principles. Some Indigenous groups have used social economy approaches to advance food sovereignty and rebuild community sustenance. One study argues that an Indigenous social economy combined with the power of food can decolonize, eradicate inequities, and rebuild community health (Sumner, McMurtry, & Tarhan, 2023). At the same time, scholars caution that the social economy sector has much work to do to reconcile with Indigenous communities. Historical injustices, including laws that were racialized and colonial in nature, have created deep inequities that the social economy alone cannot resolve. Some researchers question whether the social economy can truly serve Indigenous communities without confronting these colonial legacies directly (Sumner et al., 2023).

Key Political Issues: Federal Policy and Recognition

A central political issue is the absence of a coherent federal policy framework for the social economy. While Quebec has its own legislation and action plans, the federal government has no equivalent law. Federal support has come in the form of pilot programs, research funding, and occasional budget allocations rather than a sustained strategy. The federal Budget 2025 introduced a Buy Canadian Policy that aims to ensure federal procurement supports Canadian social enterprises, including cooperatives (Co-operatives and Mutuals Canada, 2025). This is a positive step, but the social economy remains peripheral to most federal economic policy. Federal social procurement policy, managed by Public Services and Procurement Canada, now facilitates the inclusion of socio-economic measures in procurements. However, the scale and impact of these measures remain limited compared to the sector's potential. Advocates continue to call for a national social economy strategy that would provide stable funding, regulatory recognition, and a seat at the policy table.

Key Political Issues: Inequality and Affordability

The social economy in Canada operates within a context of deepening inequality and an affordability crisis that makes its mission more urgent and more difficult. As of early 2026, one in four Canadians lived in a food-insecure household. The proportion of people reporting financial stress rose from 30 percent to 44 percent over two years (Food Banks Canada, 2026). The wealthiest one percent of Canadians hold almost as much wealth as the bottom 80 percent combined. In 2025, Canada was home to approximately 89 billionaires, and the wealth of the richest 40 grew by nearly $95 billion in a single year. At the same time, hundreds of thousands experienced homelessness (Oxfam Canada, 2026). The gap between rich and poor reached a record high in 2025. This extreme concentration of wealth weakens economic security, social cohesion, and democracy itself. The social economy offers a partial response by creating jobs, providing services, and keeping resources in communities. But it cannot substitute for public policies that address the root causes of inequality.

Key Political Issues: The Social Safety Net and Precarious Work

The condition of Canada's social safety net is another major political issue that shapes the social economy. Employment Insurance and social assistance programs have been criticized as outdated and inadequate for the realities of precarious and underemployed work. A 2026 report found that two-parent families with full-time workers are among those turning to food banks, revealing that gaps in income security affect not only the unemployed but also the working poor (CTV News, 2026). The federal government has introduced measures such as the Canada Disability Benefit and a National School Food Program. It has also initiated a working group on a guaranteed livable basic income with the government of Prince Edward Island (Senate of Canada, 2025). These developments suggest growing recognition that the current safety net is insufficient. However, the pace of reform remains slow. Social economy organizations often fill the gaps left by inadequate public programs, providing food, housing, and employment supports. This role brings stability to communities but also creates a risk that the social economy becomes a permanent substitute for public responsibility.

The Role of Procurement and Public Policy Tools

Procurement policy has emerged as a practical tool for supporting the social economy. Social procurement is the practice of using purchasing power to achieve socio-economic objectives alongside the delivery of goods and services. The federal government's Policy on Social Procurement facilitates the inclusion of socio-economic measures in Public Services and Procurement Canada's acquisitions (Public Services and Procurement Canada, 2026). In Quebec, the Social Economy Act permits public bodies to grant a preferential margin to social economy enterprises in procurement processes (Social Economy Act, 2013). In British Columbia, social purchasing guidelines allow purchasers to consider social impact in service contracts over $75,000 (Government of British Columbia, 2025). These measures represent a shift away from the traditional understanding of best value as solely financial. They recognize that every purchase has economic, environmental, cultural, and social consequences. However, social procurement remains uneven across jurisdictions and sectors. Many social enterprises still find it difficult to navigate complex procurement processes and compete with larger private firms.

Internal Debates: Social Economy or Solidarity Economy

An important debate within and beyond the sector concerns terminology itself. Some scholars and practitioners argue that the term social economy is limited in what it means to people of the African diaspora and other racialized communities, who have had to struggle and fight for economic recognition. These voices advocate for the social economy sector in Canada to adopt the term solidarity economy, which encompasses conflict and the need for systemic change (The Banker Ladies, 2024). The solidarity economy framework places greater emphasis on challenging power structures, confronting oppression, and building alternatives that are explicitly transformative. In contrast, the social economy framework has been criticized for being more reformist and for accommodating itself too comfortably within existing capitalist structures. This debate is not merely semantic. It reflects deeper questions about whether the social economy should aim to improve conditions within the current system or to build a fundamentally different economic order. The global network RIPESS, which CCEDNet participates in, uses the combined term social and solidarity economy, acknowledging both traditions.

The Current Landscape and Future Prospects

The social economy in Canada today is a diverse and evolving sector. It includes long-established cooperatives and credit unions, large non-profit organizations, small community enterprises, and emerging social ventures. It operates in every province and territory, in urban and rural settings, and across sectors from housing and healthcare to food and finance. In Quebec, it is recognized by law and supported by a comprehensive policy architecture. Outside Quebec, it remains less institutionalized but is growing in visibility and impact. The sector faces significant challenges. Access to stable financing remains a persistent barrier. Public procurement processes are often poorly adapted to social enterprise models. The absence of a national policy framework creates uncertainty and uneven development. The broader context of extreme wealth inequality and an inadequate social safety net places heavy demands on social economy organizations. Yet the sector also demonstrates remarkable resilience and innovation. Social enterprises continue to emerge, communities continue to organize, and advocacy for recognition and support continues at local, provincial, and national levels. The future of the social economy in Canada will depend on whether governments at all levels choose to treat it as a genuine partner in building a fairer and more sustainable economy, or whether it remains a patchwork of local initiatives filling gaps that public policy has failed to address.
