Introduction to the Social and Solidarity Economy in Japan

The social and solidarity economy (SSE) in Japan encompasses a wide range of organizations and practices that prioritize social objectives over pure profit, including cooperatives, non-profit organizations, social enterprises, and mutual aid groups. While Japan has deep-rooted traditions of mutual assistance and community support, the concept of SSE as a distinct economic sector remains relatively under-recognized in policy discourse and the broader enterprise landscape (Itami, 2025). This article examines the historical foundations, current state, and political challenges facing the social economy and solidarity movement in Japan.

Historical Foundations of Mutual Aid and Cooperation

Japan's tradition of cooperative and mutual aid organizations predates modern legal frameworks by centuries. Village cooperatives developed entirely outside the framework of public administration or legal regulation, operating on moral contracts of mutual protection against misfortune (Najita, 1996). These institutions functioned over hundreds of years and reflected an ethic of reverence for life that was neither purely traditional nor modern. The philosophy of cooperatives began to take more formal shape in the mid-nineteenth century, and the Industrial Cooperative Law of 1900 marked a significant milestone by enabling agricultural producers, forestry owners, fishermen, and consumers to organize cooperatives across the country (Permanent Mission of Japan to the United Nations, n.d.). By 1923, Japanese cooperatives had 2.6 million members, placing the country among the world's leading centres of cooperativism.

The Postwar Welfare Society Model

The postwar period fundamentally reshaped Japan's approach to social solidarity. The Japanese Constitution of 1945 included social rights but tethered them to an older concept of the "right to existence" (seizonken) (Jensen & Walton, 2022). While efforts were made to investigate working-class conditions and devise favourable social policies, strong opposition to unionism, socialism, and the welfare state directed these efforts toward a non-state model of social solidarity. This model saw the individual as belonging primarily to a company and family, evolving into what came to be called a "welfare society" by the late 1970s. Notably, only full-time male workers receiving monthly salaries benefited from the socio-economic policies of the immediate post-war era, while women were excluded (Jensen & Walton, 2022). This exclusion created structural inequalities that would have lasting consequences for the precariat class in subsequent decades.

The Emergence of Worker Cooperatives

The worker cooperative movement in Japan emerged from the post-World War II "Relief Measures for the Unemployed" program in 1949. The Japan Free Workers' Union was formed in 1953 and later established numerous business enterprises to provide stable employment for its members (Nakano, 2026). These enterprises evolved into worker cooperatives influenced by European models, culminating in the formation of the Japan Workers' Cooperative Union in 1993. This union played a crucial role in advocating for and ultimately achieving the enactment of the Worker Cooperative Act in 2020, the first new cooperative act in Japan in 42 years (Nakano, 2026). The Act defines worker cooperatives, establishes their legal framework, and promotes their role in creating sustainable and vibrant communities, while the union continues to expand its network and promote the concept of "associated work" as a democratic and participatory work model.

Non-Profit Organizations and Legal Frameworks

The legal framework for non-profit organizations in Japan has evolved significantly over recent decades. The Act on Promotion of Specified Non-Profit Activities, enacted in 1998, grants legal personality to organizations engaging in specified non-profit activities and establishes a system for their approval (Act on Promotion of Specified Non-Profit Activities, 1998). This legislation aims to promote the sound development of specified non-profit activities as free social contribution activities by citizens, including volunteer activities, and to contribute to the enhancement of public interest. The NPO law includes an information disclosure system that is unique among Japanese legal frameworks, premised on citizen choice and monitoring through information disclosure (City of Yokohama, 2026). However, eligibility for donation-related tax benefits remains narrowly defined and subject to strict conditions, which has been criticized as a barrier to the development of a donation culture (International Center for Not-for-Profit Law, 2026).

Key Organizations and Platforms in the SSE Landscape

Several prominent organizations form the backbone of Japan's SSE landscape. The Social Enterprise Research Association, which operated for 15 years, was reorganized into the Japan Forum for the Promotion of Social and Solidarity Economy in 2022. This platform brings together researchers and practitioners to advance SSE principles (Fujii, 2025). Within the forum's membership, the Seikatsu Club Consumers' Cooperative Group is considered the organization most closely aligned with SSE values in Japan. The Seikatsu Club combines business and production with strict social and ecological principles and a vision of a community-centred economy (Right Livelihood, 2025). The total worth of the Seikatsu Club Group's welfare programs has reached 17.3 billion yen, one of the largest for a corporate group in Japan. Other significant actors include Palsystem Consumers' Co-operative Union and the Workers' Collective Network, which advocates for individuals with disabilities (Fujii, 2025).

Government Policy and Political Recognition

Government policy toward the social economy has evolved in recent years. The "Grand Design and Action Plan for a New Form of Capitalism," approved by the Cabinet in 2023, positions the creation of "zebra enterprises" that solve local social challenges as a key priority (Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, 2025). This policy framework also appears in the "Basic Policy on Economic and Fiscal Management and Reform 2025" and the "Regional Revitalization 2.0 Basic Concept," both approved in June 2025. The government aims to create and nurture enterprises that address regional social issues and attract impact investment, thereby promoting a multi-stakeholder corporate society that considers social and environmental impacts alongside financial risk and return. Local governments have also implemented their own support programs, such as the Setagaya Ward Social Business Support Subsidy, which provides financial assistance to private operators working on social business initiatives that address regional and social challenges (Setagaya City, 2026).

Structural Challenges Facing the SSE

Despite these developments, the SSE remains relatively under-recognized in Japan's policy discourse, enterprise landscape, and world of work. The International Labour Organization report on decent work and the SSE in Japan highlights several structural and institutional challenges affecting SSE development. These include fragmented legal and policy frameworks, limited public awareness, and weak coordination among SSE actors (Itami, 2025). The report, based on dialogues with government representatives, social partners, SSE entities, and academics, identifies these challenges as significant barriers to the sector's growth. There is also a notable gap between the well-established practices of cooperation and mutual aid that exist across the country and the lack of formal policy recognition and support for SSE as a distinct economic model.

Demographic Pressures and the Social Economy

Japan's severe demographic challenges present both obstacles and opportunities for the social economy. The country is experiencing unprecedented population decline, with births falling to a record low of 705,809 in 2025, a decrease of 15,179 from the previous year and the tenth consecutive annual decline (Komei Party, 2026). Population decline threatens to trigger a "shrinking spiral" of domestic market contraction, reduced capital investment, innovation stagnation, and productivity decline. The working-age population is projected to decrease by 17 million from its current level of 75 million to 2040, representing a loss of approximately 20 percent. Regional areas are particularly affected, with many municipalities experiencing the outflow of young people and resulting population decline. This demographic crisis creates urgent needs for social services, particularly in healthcare, long-term care, and welfare, where labour shortages are already evident across all sectors (Komei Party, 2026).

Poverty and Inequality in Contemporary Japan

Poverty and inequality have emerged as pressing political issues in Japan, exposing gaps in the social safety net. In urban areas such as Shinjuku in Tokyo, long queues form outside free food distribution events organized by civil society organizations. These distributions, which have continued weekly for over six years, now serve not only homeless individuals but also a growing number of working people who cannot maintain a decent standard of living despite being employed (China Youth Network, 2026). The food assistance includes bread, bananas, tomatoes, compressed biscuits, and instant rice, alongside counselling, health guidance, and legal aid services. This phenomenon reflects the expansion of the precariat class, a development that scholars trace back to the postwar welfare society model that excluded significant portions of the population from full social rights (Jensen & Walton, 2022). The policy emphasis on military expansion has been criticized for diverting resources away from addressing these fundamental social welfare needs (Guangming Daily, 2026).

Labour Market Dualism and Social Protection Gaps

Labour market reforms need to continue as the share of women and older workers in non-regular employment remains high in Japan (OECD, 2026). The OECD Economic Survey of Japan 2026 recommends boosting the flexibility of regular employment contracts to help break down labour market dualism. Providing relevant and high-quality adult learning programs targeted toward older workers and workers on non-standard contracts is necessary to engage them in quality employment. The survey also notes that while Japan's economy has shown resilience, with output expanding at a moderate pace driven by domestic demand, reforms to ensure fiscal sustainability and boost productivity and labour supply need to be continued to address demographic and external headwinds. Strengthening work incentives for older workers and women would help boost labour supply, while cutting administrative burdens would lift business productivity (OECD, 2026).

The Role of Impact Investment and Social Finance

The development of impact investment and social finance mechanisms represents a significant area of policy interest. The Keizai Doyukai, in collaboration with the Impact Startup Association and the Japan Philanthropic Association, has proposed measures to facilitate the flow of funds between corporations and the social sector (Keizai Doyukai, 2026). Their recommendations include establishing a fund to collect donations from corporations and provide grants to NPOs, amending the Corporate Governance Code to include contributions to solving social issues as a management resource allocation theme, and expanding donation tax incentives to allow deductions of up to 10 percent of taxable income with carry-forward provisions for five years. The proposals note that corporate donations in Japan stood at 1.4 trillion yen in fiscal 2023, representing only 0.2 percent of nominal GDP, and that total donations including individual giving are only about one-fifth of the level in the United States (Keizai Doyukai, 2026). Social sector organizations identify human resource recruitment and fundraising as their primary challenges, making the facilitation of corporate funding flows an urgent priority.

Governance and Political Tensions

Political tensions have emerged around the direction of social and economic policy in Japan. Critics argue that the government's focus on military expansion has diverted attention and resources from addressing structural policy imbalances that contribute to poverty and inequality (China Youth Network, 2026). The aging of the population, industrial transformation, and policy choices have combined to worsen poverty, while successive governments have been accused of ignoring long-standing structural policy failures. The policy focus and the practical demands of the public appear to be misaligned, which has been identified as a core source of deepening social division. Additionally, the rise of right-wing political forces and their influence on policy have been described as significant factors exacerbating these contradictions, as the government has prioritized military expenditure over social welfare spending (Guangming Daily, 2026).

Regional Revitalization and Local SSE Initiatives

Regional revitalization has become an important arena for SSE development. The government's Regional Revitalization 2.0 Basic Concept emphasizes the role of local zebra enterprises as important actors in solving regional social issues and creating attractive local jobs, especially for young people and women (Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, 2025). Various forms of local initiatives are being explored, including the use of community currencies, employment creation adapted to changing regional conditions, and integrated approaches to poverty and educational inequality through public-private partnerships. Organizations such as the NPO Machizukuri Network Kitashirakawa in Osaka and Town Space WAKWAK in Takatsuki are cited as examples of locally rooted SSE practice (PARC, 2025). These initiatives demonstrate the potential of SSE to address contemporary societal challenges, from job creation and social inclusion to sustainable local development, though they remain constrained by limited resources and recognition.

Conclusion and Future Directions

The social economy and solidarity sector in Japan stands at a crossroads. It possesses deep historical roots in mutual aid traditions and a growing number of dedicated organizations and practitioners. Recent policy developments, including the Worker Cooperative Act of 2020 and government support for zebra enterprises, indicate increasing recognition of the sector's potential. However, significant challenges remain. The SSE concept itself is still relatively under-recognized in policy discourse, legal frameworks remain fragmented, public awareness is limited, and coordination among actors is weak (Itami, 2025). The pressing demographic crisis, rising poverty, and labour market dualism create both urgent needs and opportunities for the sector to demonstrate its value. Whether Japan can develop a more coherent and supportive policy environment for the social and solidarity economy will determine the extent to which these alternative economic models can contribute to addressing the country's profound social and economic challenges.

article:
Introduction to Kenya's Social Economy

Kenya has one of the most vibrant social and solidarity economies in Africa. This economy is built on traditions of mutual aid, community self-help, and collective resource pooling that predate colonialism. Today, the social economy in Kenya includes cooperatives, savings groups, social enterprises, and community-based organizations. These entities prioritize people and purpose over pure profit. The government has recently begun to formally recognize this sector as a key driver of inclusive development. In 2025, Kenya hosted the first regional forum on the African Union's ten-year strategy for the social and solidarity economy, signaling a new level of political commitment to this model (Ministry of MSMEs Development, 2025).

Historical Roots of Solidarity

The roots of Kenya's social economy run deep. Before colonial rule, Kenyan communities practiced traditions of collective work and sharing. Labor-sharing groups, known by names such as mweria, brought neighbors together to farm land, build homes, and support one another during difficult times (Ruddick, 2025). These practices were not charity. They were structured systems of reciprocity and mutual obligation. The harambee spirit, which means "pulling together" in Swahili, grew from these older traditions. When Kenya gained independence in 1963, the first president, Jomo Kenyatta, adopted harambee as a national slogan for self-reliant development. Between 1963 and 1988, harambee efforts mobilized more than US$55 million for schools, health centers, and other community projects (BBC, 2020).

Cooperatives in the Colonial and Post-Colonial Era

Cooperatives became a formal expression of the social economy during the colonial period. African farmers and traders used cooperatives to pool resources and gain access to markets that were otherwise closed to them. These cooperatives created bridges between the informal rural economy and the formal sector (Musundi, 2026). Women played important roles in these early cooperatives. For example, Women's Poultry Keepers' societies and pottery-making groups gave African women a rare space for economic participation in a colonial system that often excluded them from formal statistics (Musundi, 2026). After independence, cooperatives grew rapidly. By 1990, cooperatives in Kenya controlled approximately 40 percent of the gross national product, and by 2005, there were roughly 3.3 million cooperative members in the country (Musundi, 2026).

The Harambee Movement and Its Political Dimensions

The harambee movement became the centerpiece of Kenya's post-independence development strategy. It was a hybrid model that combined community self-reliance with state support (Holmquist, 1984, as cited in Ruddick, 2025). Communities would organize themselves and mobilize resources for local projects, and the government would sometimes provide matching funds or technical assistance. However, the movement was not without its problems. Over time, harambee became associated with corruption and the co-optation of local efforts by politicians for personal gain. The success of projects often depended on having good connections to politicians and government resources (Ruddick, 2025). This "half-way" character, neither fully self-reliant nor fully state-initiated, created tensions that continue to shape debates about the social economy today.

Social Protection and National Solidarity

Kenya was one of the first African countries to develop national social protection legislation after independence. The National Social Security Fund was created in 1965, and the National Hospital Insurance Fund followed in 1967 (UNOSSC, 2019). These programs represented a vision of national solidarity, where citizens contribute to a shared pool that protects everyone against life's risks. However, the structural adjustment programs of the 1980s and 1990s weakened these systems. Government spending on social sectors dropped, and many Kenyans became more vulnerable (UNOSSC, 2019). In recent years, Kenya has revived its commitment to social protection. The government has piloted a Universal Basic Income experiment and has embraced new partnerships between the public and private sectors (UNOSSC, 2019).

Informal Financial Groups and Community Resilience

Informal financial groups are perhaps the most widespread expression of the solidarity economy in Kenya. These include chamas, which are rotating savings and credit associations, and saccos, which are savings and credit cooperatives. Chamas are typically small groups of friends, neighbors, or colleagues who meet regularly to contribute money that is then given to one member at a time. This system allows people who lack access to formal banking to save and access lump sums for school fees, medical bills, or business start-ups (Ruddick, 2025). The chama model has proven remarkably resilient. It adapts to the needs of its members and operates on trust and social accountability rather than collateral. In refugee communities and informal urban settlements, these groups are often the primary source of financial services (Grassroots Economics Foundation, 2025).

Grassroots Economics and Commitment Pooling

One of the most innovative expressions of the solidarity economy in Kenya is the work of the Grassroots Economics Foundation. This Kenya-based nonprofit works with marginalized communities to build localized, regenerative economic systems. Its approach begins not with financial capital but with collective trust and ancestral knowledge (Grassroots Economics Foundation, 2025). The foundation facilitates a practice called Commitment Pooling. This is a system of community-led resource coordination inspired by traditional labor-sharing structures such as mweria and harambee. Communities create registries of commitments, where members record what they can offer, such as labor, food, or care, and what they need. These commitments are then exchanged through mutual aid networks rather than through cash (Grassroots Economics Foundation, 2025). This model enables communities to meet needs that mainstream monetary systems fail to address.

Political Issues Facing the Social Economy

The social economy in Kenya operates within a complex and often challenging political environment. One major issue is the tension between state control and community autonomy. Throughout Kenya's history, self-help movements have been both a tool of resistance against state power and a vehicle for state control (Ruddick, 2025). The colonial government used community development schemes to win over opposition, while independence governments used harambee to extend their reach into rural areas. This "double-edged political sword" means that grassroots organizations must constantly navigate their relationship with the state (Holmquist, 1984, as cited in Ruddick, 2025). Today, many social economy organizations seek to maintain their independence while also accessing government support and recognition.

Economic Inequality and Its Impact

Economic inequality is a profound challenge for Kenya's social economy. A 2025 report by Oxfam Kenya revealed that the richest one percent of the population controls 78 percent of the country's total financial wealth (Oxfam Kenya, 2025, as cited in Pulse, 2025). Persistent extreme poverty affects 46 percent of Kenyans (Ministry of Devolution, 2025). These disparities undermine social solidarity. When wealth is concentrated in the hands of a few, the sense of shared fate that underpins the social economy is weakened. The UN Kenya Common Country Analysis 2025 Update noted that poverty, inequality, and regional disparities persist, especially in arid and semi-arid counties (UN Kenya, 2025). The report also highlighted that climate shocks, including recurring droughts and floods, intensify existing vulnerabilities. Ten counties remain most at risk, including Mandera, Wajir, Garissa, Turkana, and West Pokot (UN Kenya, 2025).

Public Debt and Fiscal Pressures

Kenya's high public debt is another significant political issue that affects the social economy. The country's public debt stands at nearly 70 percent of gross domestic product, and debt servicing costs consume over a third of government revenues (Carnegie Endowment, 2026). In just four years, interest on public debt jumped from 18 percent to 25 percent of total spending, draining money from essential services (Kenya Human Rights Commission, 2025). The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights has raised questions about Kenya's high level of country debt and the regressive response to social protests (OHCHR, 2026). The committee noted that while Kenya has developed its social protection system over the last decade, including the adoption of the Social Protection Bill 2025, the debt burden threatens these gains.

Social Protests and State Response

The political environment has been marked by social protests, particularly among young people. In June, July, and August 2024, Kenya experienced significant protests. The UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights received "extremely worrying information about the repressive State response" to these protests, which "culminated in numerous deaths and injuries, enforced disappearances, kidnappings, torture, and cases of arbitrary detentions" (OHCHR, 2026). The committee asked what measures were being taken to prevent and end the illegal repression of social protest and the persecution of human rights defenders. The Kenyan delegation acknowledged that the country had challenges with protests and stated that young people had a right to protest but it needed to be peaceful (OHCHR, 2026). This tension between protest and state response is a critical issue for the social economy, which depends on civic space and freedom of association.

The Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda

The Kenyan government has articulated a development vision called the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda, or BETA. This agenda aims to democratize economic opportunities and support grassroots enterprises (Ministry of MSMEs Development, 2025). Under BETA, the government has launched several programs that align with social economy principles. The Uwezo Fund and the Hustler Fund provide financial support to women, youth, and vulnerable populations (Ministry of MSMEs Development, 2025). The Hustler Fund, in particular, is designed to provide small loans to informal sector workers who lack access to traditional banking. However, critics have noted that the "hustler narrative" celebrates individual grit without building the institutional support that a true social market economy requires (Konrad-Adenauer-Stiftung, 2024). Some argue that Kenya needs architectural redesign, not just motivational rhetoric, to transform hustle into sustainable prosperity.

The African Union Strategy on Social and Solidarity Economy

At the continental level, the African Union adopted a ten-year strategy on the Social and Solidarity Economy in February 2025. This strategy aligns with the 2023 UN Resolution on SSE, which recognized the critical role of the social economy in achieving sustainable development (Ministry of MSMEs Development, 2025). Kenya has positioned itself as a leader in this continental effort. In 2025, the Ministry of MSMEs Development hosted the first regional high-level forum on the implementation of the AU strategy. The Cabinet Secretary for Labour and Social Protection, Dr. Alfred Mutua, emphasized Kenya's long-standing tradition of social and solidarity economies, deeply rooted in community structures such as chamas and saccos (Ministry of MSMEs Development, 2025). He noted that the government is now embedding this model into national policy.

Conclusion

The social economy and solidarity in Kenya represent a rich and complex tradition. From pre-colonial labor-sharing practices to modern cooperatives, savings groups, and social enterprises, Kenyans have long relied on collective action to meet their needs. The harambee spirit, despite its political complications, remains a powerful cultural force. The chama model continues to provide financial services to millions who are excluded from formal banking. Innovative organizations like the Grassroots Economics Foundation are experimenting with new forms of community currency and commitment pooling. However, the social economy faces significant challenges. Economic inequality, public debt, political repression of protests, and the tension between state control and community autonomy all threaten its vitality. The government's BETA agenda and the African Union's SSE strategy offer opportunities for the social economy to grow and gain recognition. Whether these opportunities are seized will depend on the ability of communities, civil society, and the state to work together in genuine solidarity.

article:
Historical Roots and Cultural Foundations

The social and solidarity economy (SSE) in the Philippines is not a new concept imported from abroad. It is deeply rooted in Filipino culture and traditions of mutual aid. Practices such as bayanihan (collective community work), damayan (reciprocity), and pagutulungan (helping one another) have long embodied the principles of cooperation and shared responsibility that define the SSE today (ILO, 2021). These cultural values provided fertile ground for the development of formal cooperative structures when the idea was first introduced to the country. Cooperativism in the Philippines began in the 19th century, when Filipino travelers to Europe, including national hero Dr. Jose P. Rizal, brought back the concept of economic cooperation. Exiled in Dapitan, Rizal himself set up a cooperative-based school and store for the poor (Cooperative Development Authority, 2013).

The Formalization of Cooperatives

The formal cooperative movement took shape in the early 20th century. The first rural credit cooperative was established in 1915, marking the beginning of organized cooperative development (ILO, n.d.). However, progress was slow and uneven. By 1972, of the more than 6,000 cooperatives registered by the government, only about 25 percent were considered viable (ILO, n.d.). The movement gained renewed attention after the agrarian reform program was revitalized in 1972, which led to the creation of thousands of Samahang Nayon (village associations) across the country (World Bank, n.d.). A major turning point came after the 1986 People's Power Revolution that ousted the Marcos regime. The 1987 Constitution explicitly recognized the right of independent people's organizations to organize and mobilize, and it promoted the role of cooperatives, community-based organizations, and non-governmental organizations in economic and social development (ILO, 2021).

The Modern SSE Landscape

Today, the Philippines has one of the most vibrant SSE landscapes in Southeast Asia. The sector encompasses a wide range of organizations, including cooperatives, social enterprises, people's organizations, non-governmental organizations, micro-finance institutions, and community-based enterprises (ILO, 2021). The cooperative movement alone is a major economic force, with nearly 13 million members and thousands of registered cooperatives nationwide (Coop Chamber, 2025). Social enterprises have also proliferated. According to a 2019 Asian Development Bank report, there are more than 164,000 social enterprises in the country, and approximately 70 percent of them are micro, small, and medium enterprises (Dacanay, as cited in BusinessWorld, 2026). These enterprises operate across diverse sectors, including agriculture, retail, manufacturing, and services.

Cooperatives as a Pillar of the Social Economy

Cooperatives form the backbone of the social and solidarity economy in the Philippines. They are distinct from conventional corporations because they are owned and democratically controlled by their members, who share in the surplus generated by the enterprise. The Philippine Cooperative Code of 2008 (Republic Act No. 9520) provides the legal framework for their operation. A core principle enshrined in the Code is "one member, one vote," which ensures that control rests with members rather than with capital (Cooperative Development Authority, n.d.). This democratic structure is central to the cooperative identity. As the Philippine Chamber of Cooperatives has argued, cooperatives are "social justice enterprises mandated by the Constitution to foster self-reliance among the marginalized" (Coop Chamber, 2026).

Social Enterprises and Inclusive Growth

Social enterprises represent another key component of the SSE. These are mission-driven organizations that create wealth while contributing to social well-being and ecological sustainability (BusinessWorld, 2026). Unlike traditional businesses, social enterprises prioritize their social mission alongside or above profit. They often work with poor and marginalized communities, integrating them into value chains as producers, suppliers, or consumers. Research from the Philippine Institute for Development Studies notes that social enterprises have been emerging as alternative organizations to achieve inclusive and sustainable growth, demonstrating that firms can be vehicles for both profit and moral imperatives (Ballesteros & Llanto, 2017). A successful example is found in Negros Occidental, where a community-based enterprise assisted more than 300 households across 11 villages in increasing their income through collective production and marketing (Canares, 2013).

The Policy Environment

The policy environment for the SSE in the Philippines is a mix of strong constitutional foundations and fragmented implementation. The 1987 Constitution provided important recognition for people's organizations and cooperatives. Since then, various laws and programs have been introduced to support SSE organizations (ILO, 2021). However, the current policy environment remains largely unresponsive to the specific needs and growth of social enterprises (Ballesteros & Llanto, 2017). One of the most significant legislative efforts is the Poverty Reduction Through Social Entrepreneurship (PRESENT) Act. This proposed measure aims to provide social enterprises with better access to financing through non-collateralized loans and a government-supported guarantee fund pool (BusinessWorld, 2026). It also seeks to establish incentives such as tax exemptions and preferential treatment in government procurement. Several versions of the bill have been filed in both the Senate and the House of Representatives, but they remain pending at the committee level (Senate of the Philippines, 2025).

Political Issues: Taxation and Fiscal Policy

Taxation is a major political battleground for the SSE. In 2026, the Philippine Chamber of Cooperatives expressed strong opposition to an OECD recommendation to phase out Value Added Tax exemptions for cooperatives and essential social services (Coop Chamber, 2026). The Chamber argued that in a country where social transfer mechanisms are still being modernized, the VAT exemption functions as the most immediate and effective subsidy for vulnerable groups. Removing it would increase the cost of living and potentially widen the inequality gap. The Chamber also cautioned against categorizing cooperative tax privileges as "fiscal incentives" that require rationalization, noting that cooperatives return their surplus to members to aid in their livelihood, and taxing this surplus would penalize the very financial inclusion that the state seeks to promote (Coop Chamber, 2026).

Political Issues: Cooperative Governance and the Revised Code

Another critical political issue is the proposed revision of the Philippine Cooperative Code. In 2026, the Senate approved Senate Bill No. 1431, which seeks to modernize the rules governing cooperatives. One of its notable provisions would allow foreign investments in cooperatives, subject to safeguards ensuring Filipino control and management (PNA, 2026). The measure also aims to streamline registration and expand the types and activities of cooperatives. However, the Philippine Chamber of Cooperatives has raised concerns about proposals to introduce share-based voting in federations and secondary cooperatives (Coop Chamber, 2025). The Chamber argues that tying voting power to capital would compromise the sector's core identity and hand democratic control to the few. It has firmly advocated for maintaining the "one member, one vote" principle, warning that share-based voting would turn cooperatives into corporations (Coop Chamber, 2025).

Challenges Facing the SSE

Despite its vibrancy, the SSE sector in the Philippines faces significant challenges. Access to finance remains a persistent obstacle. Many social enterprises and cooperatives struggle to secure funding from traditional financial institutions due to a lack of collateral (BusinessWorld, 2026). The ecosystem for social enterprises is also described as underdeveloped, fragmented, and loosely defined (PIDS, 2026). The lack of a harmonized definition and inclusive certification system creates regulatory uncertainty and opens space for issues such as "social washing," where businesses claim social impact without clear accountability (PIDS, 2026). Additionally, many social enterprises face capacity-building challenges, with limited resources for training and strengthening internal systems, particularly for enterprises based in remote areas (BusinessMirror, 2025).

Vulnerability and Economic Precariousness

The SSE operates within a broader context of economic vulnerability in the Philippines. According to the World Bank, nearly 28 percent of Filipinos are vulnerable or remain at risk of falling back into poverty (World Bank, 2026). The typical Filipino family earns just enough to stay above the poverty line but not enough to feel economically secure. With 61 percent of the population at high risk from climate-related disasters and most families having no savings or insurance, a single typhoon, hospital bill, or lost job can push a family back into poverty (World Bank, 2026). Only one in three Filipino workers contributes to social security, leaving the vast majority unprotected in old age or job loss. These conditions make the social protection and mutual aid functions of SSE organizations particularly vital.

Resilience and Disaster Response

SSE organizations play a crucial role in building community resilience, especially in the face of disasters. The International Labour Organization has partnered with CLIMBS, a cooperative insurer with thousands of member cooperatives, to extend mutual protection and microinsurance to poor and vulnerable communities (ILO, 2025). This collaboration helps communities manage climate- and disaster-related risks. The ILO also engages with the cooperative movement through platforms such as the International Conference on Cooperatives in the Philippines, promoting cooperatives' role in resilience, social protection, and sustainable development (ILO, 2025). Community-based enterprises have proven capable of helping local associations reach national and international markets, achieve economic, social, and environmental benefits, and even manage natural resources collectively (Canares, 2013).

The Role of Informal Workers

A less visible but important part of the SSE involves organizations of informal workers. Networks such as PATAMABA, Homenet Philippines, and MAGCAISA have organized home-based workers and other informal economy workers to advocate for their rights (UNRISD, 2013). One of their key initiatives is the push for a Magna Carta for Workers in the Informal Economy (MACWIE), which aims to provide legal recognition and protection for workers who fall outside the formal labor market (UNRISD, 2013). These organizations represent a form of solidarity economy that emerges from the ground up, addressing the needs of workers who are often excluded from both traditional employment protections and formal SSE structures.

Looking Ahead

The future of the social and solidarity economy in the Philippines depends on several factors. Strengthening the policy environment is essential. The passage of the PRESENT Act would provide a significant boost by addressing the financing constraints that hold back many social enterprises (BusinessWorld, 2026). The revision of the Cooperative Code must balance modernization with the preservation of democratic principles that define the sector. Building a clearer ecosystem for social enterprises, with a harmonized definition and inclusive certification system, would help build trust and prevent social washing (PIDS, 2026). Finally, greater investment in capacity-building and access to finance for grassroots organizations would enable the SSE to reach its full potential as a driver of inclusive and sustainable development. As the World Bank has noted, with the right policy mix, the Philippines can all but eliminate poverty by 2040 and build a secure middle class (World Bank, 2026). The social and solidarity economy, with its deep roots in Filipino culture and its demonstrated capacity to reach the marginalized, will be an essential partner in that journey.

article:
Historical Roots of Solidarity in Senegal

The social and solidarity economy in Senegal is not a new idea imported from elsewhere. It rests on a long tradition of mutual aid and collective work that existed long before the modern concept of SSE was introduced. In precolonial times, land and resource management followed collective, family, and kinship rules that were specific to each community (World Bank, 2020). People organized community fields, group work for collective or individual goals, and shared systems of social security such as grandmothers caring for children near the fields and collective support for funerals, weddings, and baptisms (Fall, 2015). These practices formed the foundation of what would later be called the social and solidarity economy.

The formal history of SSE in Senegal goes back to 1875, when the colonial administration set up the Sociétés Indigènes de Prévoyance, or Indigenous Providence Societies. These were designed to provide food and seed security for peasants and to keep the peanut economy running smoothly (Gellar, 2005). This colonial institution was not a grassroots cooperative. It was a state tool. Unlike Western cooperatives that emerged when individual farmers banded together to improve their bargaining power, the cooperative movement in Senegal was largely created by the state (Gellar, 2005). This top-down origin would shape the sector for decades to come.

The Post-Independence Cooperative Movement

After Senegal gained independence in 1960, two ideological currents clashed among the ruling elite. One was the assimilationist camp led by President Léopold Sédar Senghor, who favored a model of catching up with the West. The other was the nationalist camp led by Prime Minister Mamadou Dia, who wanted to build a socialist state (ILO, 2021). The cooperative movement became a key lever for Dia's nationalist project in favor of the popular classes. The idea was for cooperatives to allow members to pool resources, buy what they needed, and sell their products without depending on middlemen who profited from agricultural trade (ILO, 2021).

The government launched a national cooperative program that aimed to mobilize rural populations behind national development policies and a communitarian socialist ideology (Gellar, 2005). Cooperatives were supposed to be an extension of local traditions of community solidarity. In practice, however, they developed under heavy state control. Government officials imposed the cooperative model instead of letting it grow naturally, and the movement suffered from a lack of founding autonomy (ILO, 2021). After Mamadou Dia left power, the cooperative sector continued but with less ideological drive. In 1960 and 1961, the state embarked on a bold reform of the cooperative system, refashioning local village cooperatives and sending rural animators to teach peasants new cooperative values (Gellar, 2005).

The Rise of Modern SSE Policy

The concept of the social and solidarity economy as it is understood today began to take root in Senegal in the 1980s and 1990s. These decades were marked by structural adjustment programs and the withdrawal of the state from many economic activities. In this context, grassroots organizations, women's groups, and mutual health organizations stepped in to fill gaps left by the shrinking public sector. The SSE framework gained international attention through global social forums, and Senegal became a leader in the movement (Fall, 2015).

In 2017, Senegal created a Ministry of Microfinance and Social and Solidarity Economy, along with a dedicated SSE Directorate. This gave the sector an important steering mechanism and increased its visibility in public policies (UNRISD, 2021). In June 2021, the National Assembly unanimously passed the Framework Law on the Social and Solidarity Economy, Law No. 2021-28. This law introduced official definitions of SSE terms, created a National SSE Council as the national control tower for the sector, and established special tax measures favorable to SSE organizations (United Nations, 2021). The law was a major milestone because it gave SSE entities a legal identity that they had lacked before.

Government Priorities and Political Will

The current government of President Bassirou Diomaye Faye has placed the SSE at the center of its economic agenda. The President declared 2026 as the Year of the Social and Solidarity Economy in Senegal (ILO, 2026a). He has called for the full application of the framework law, including the creation of a National SSE Register and the establishment of a National SSE Council (RTS, 2026a). The government aims to build a national doctrine of endogenous development through the solidarity economy, involving public institutions, the private sector, microfinance structures, and community organizations (RTS, 2026a).

In May 2025, the Prime Minister chaired an interministerial council on the SSE that reviewed strategic axes including governance, social protection, territorial development, education, financing, and taxation. The council decided to create a National SSE Council under the supervision of the President, an Interministerial Steering Committee, a National SSE Observatory, and regional SSE services (Prime Minister's Office, 2025). The government also launched the PROGRESS program to formalize women's groups, agricultural economic interest groups, artisan small businesses, associations, and mutuals (RTS, 2026b). A key initiative is the creation of Cooperative Productives Solidaires, with the goal of establishing 10,000 of these cooperatives by 2029 (RTS, 2026c).

Key Actors and Organizations

The SSE landscape in Senegal includes a wide variety of actors. Cooperatives, mutuals, associations, and social enterprises operate in sectors ranging from agriculture and fishing to housing, health insurance, and urban mobility. In Dakar, SSE organizations have access to support structures such as the Municipal Development and Solidarity Fund and the Mutual Savings and Credit Union (UNRISD, 2021). The Network of Actors and Local Authorities for Social and Solidarity Economy brings together SSE organizations and local governments to promote the sector.

The International Labour Organization has been a major partner. Through projects like ADIJEFE, funded by Italian cooperation, the ILO has helped informal workers transform their economic interest groups into formal cooperatives. A notable example is the motorbike taxi drivers in Mbour, who created the SOCOMOYO cooperative in June 2026 with ILO support using the Think.Coop and Start.Coop tools (ILO, 2026b). The ILO has also helped integrate SSE entities into the national framework for youth professional integration, allowing cooperatives and mutuals to take on qualified young workers with state support for part of their salaries (ILO, 2026c). The National Social Mutual for Artisans of Senegal is another example of SSE actors organizing to provide social protection for informal workers (ILO, 2025).

Political Issues and Challenges

Despite strong political commitment, the SSE sector in Senegal faces serious obstacles. One major challenge is the weight of the informal economy. About 97 percent of Senegal's enterprises operate informally, and the informal sector represents around 41.6 percent of GDP (ILO, 2026d; United Nations, 2025). Most SSE organizations operate in this informal space, which limits their access to finance, taxation, and formal recognition. High interest rates and collateral requirements make it difficult for SSE organizations to obtain funding from traditional financial institutions, whose products are poorly adapted to the realities of the field (GSIF, 2020).

Access to finance remains one of the main concerns of SSE organizations. Demand far exceeds the available supply of both public and private funding (GSIF, 2020). The mechanism that reserves 5 percent of public contracts for SSE structures is poorly applied despite being written into the legal framework (ARCOP, 2025). The public procurement system does not yet fully include SSE organizations in its processes. There is also a lack of coordination between the SSE framework law and sector-specific laws in areas such as agriculture, health, and housing. This fragmentation weakens the impact of the SSE policy.

Political tensions also affect the sector. Senegal has experienced a period of political reconfiguration and institutional reform, along with growing socio-economic pressures (United Nations Senegal, 2025). Public debt reached around 100 percent of GDP in 2024, and the budget deficit exceeded 11 percent, triggering austerity measures that bear directly on social spending (ITUC, 2025). The rupture between President Faye and Prime Minister Sonko has created two competing centers of power at a critical moment for the country's reform agenda (CFR, 2025). These political tensions risk slowing down the implementation of SSE policies that require sustained coordination across ministries and levels of government.

Land Access and Other Structural Barriers

Land access is a major problem for cooperatives, especially in the Dakar region. Most cooperatives face challenges in acquiring land because the process is long, uncertain, and costly, and it is often plagued by complex transactions and fraudulent activities by developers (Reference Global, 2025). For housing cooperatives, this means that projects are delayed or abandoned. Even when land is acquired, cooperatives face challenges in managing buildings and public spaces over the long term. For agricultural cooperatives, land tenure insecurity discourages investment in productive activities.

Weak structuring of income-generating activities is another barrier. Many community initiatives remain informal and poorly organized, with insufficient technical and financial support (APS, 2026). Women's groups and youth organizations often have the energy and the local knowledge but lack the formal structures and connections needed to access markets and public programs. The government's PROGRESS program aims to address this by formalizing these groups, but the scale of the challenge is enormous. The gap between the ambition of the policy and the capacity to implement it remains wide.

The Road Ahead

The future of the social and solidarity economy in Senegal depends on whether the country can turn its strong legal and political framework into real change on the ground. The framework law of 2021 and the government's current priorities provide a solid foundation. The creation of the National SSE Register and the National SSE Council, planned for 2026, will be important steps toward giving the sector the visibility and coordination it needs (RTS, 2026a). The integration of SSE entities into youth employment policy shows that the government is willing to use the SSE as a tool for tackling unemployment (ILO, 2026c).

However, the structural challenges of informality, inadequate financing, political tensions, and weak coordination between sectors cannot be solved by laws alone. The SSE sector in Senegal needs patient investment in the capacity of its organizations, better financial products adapted to their needs, and genuine inclusion in public procurement and policy design. The tradition of solidarity that has sustained Senegalese communities for generations is a valuable asset. The question is whether public policy can nurture that tradition without smothering it, and whether the political class can maintain the stability needed to let the sector grow. The stakes are high, and the eyes of the region are on Senegal as a laboratory for the SSE in West Africa.

article:
Introduction

South Korea's social and solidarity economy (SSE) represents a distinctive model of economic organization that prioritizes reciprocity, cooperation, and community welfare alongside market exchange. The SSE encompasses diverse organizational forms including social enterprises, cooperatives, community businesses, self-sufficiency enterprises, and social ventures, all of which share a commitment to democratic governance and social value creation (GSEF, 2026). While South Korea's remarkable economic transformation from an aid recipient to a high-income economy is well documented, the parallel development of its social economy offers a less examined but equally significant narrative of institutional innovation and grassroots resilience.

Historical Background: Cooperatives Under Colonial Rule and Authoritarian Development

The modern cooperative movement in Korea began during the Japanese colonial period (1910–1945), though its origins were complex. Financial cooperatives were first established in rural areas in 1907, three years before Korea's full integration into the Japanese economy, and were later extended to urban areas in 1918 (Kwon, 2012). However, these early cooperatives were largely instruments of colonial economic control rather than autonomous community organizations. The first genuinely grassroots cooperative emerged in 1920 with the establishment of a consumer cooperative in Mokpo, founded by Korean pioneers who sought to reclaim economic rights from Japanese tradesmen and pursued political independence through economic self-reliance (ICA, n.d.). By the early 1930s, more than 290 cooperatives were active throughout the peninsula, though the Japanese colonial government's repression of collective organizing led to the dissolution of many by the 1940s (ICA, n.d.).

Following liberation and the Korean War, the cooperative movement was rebuilt but faced significant constraints under successive authoritarian regimes. The state's approach to welfare during this period was largely corporatist and employer-employee contribution based, with minimal government involvement in social provision. Self-sufficiency through employment served as the basic welfare mantra from the 1960s onward, as the state mobilized resources to bolster chaebol-led industrial development while maintaining an aversion to what was perceived as dependence-inducing welfare spending (Claassen, n.d.). The agricultural cooperative NongHyup grew into a large agribusiness and financial institution, while consumer cooperatives remained marginal until the late 1980s (ICA, n.d.). Worker cooperatives, initially suppressed after the Korean War, re-emerged only after the 1987 democratization process, driven by worker buy-outs of failing businesses, local trade union initiatives, and young people in service sectors (Eum, 2026).

The Democratization Turn and Institutional Recognition

The 1997 Asian financial crisis proved to be a watershed moment for South Korea's social economy. As the crisis exposed the vulnerabilities of the chaebol-dominated growth model and produced widespread unemployment and social dislocation, alternative economic organizations gained new legitimacy. Worker buy-outs of failing businesses became a significant pathway for cooperative formation, while the urban poor movement developed a "production community" model aimed at improving working conditions and creating an alternative economy (Eum, 2026). Influenced by the Mondragon model from Spain, Korean worker cooperatives sought solutions to challenges like limited capital, technology, and management skills, with solidarity initiatives and government self-sufficiency programmes providing crucial support.

The legal recognition of cooperatives came gradually through sector-specific legislation. Agricultural cooperatives were governed by the Agricultural Co-operatives Act of 1957, followed by laws covering forestry, small and medium enterprises, fisheries, tobacco producers, credit unions, and community credit cooperatives (ICA, n.d.). Consumer cooperatives received their own legislation in 1999. However, this fragmented legal framework proved inadequate for emerging cooperative forms such as worker cooperatives and social cooperatives, which did not fit neatly into existing categories.

The Framework Act on Cooperatives and Its Limitations

A major breakthrough came in 2011 with the passage of the Framework Act on Co-operatives, enacted to celebrate the International Year of Cooperatives (ICA, n.d.). This legislation was designed to address the restrictive nature of existing cooperative laws while acknowledging the cooperative sector's contribution to addressing challenges stemming from the global financial crisis. Under the new Act, various kinds of businesses, including those in the service industry, could form cooperatives or federations of cooperatives to provide services, including workers' cooperatives and social cooperatives (ICA, n.d.). The Korean Federation of Worker Cooperatives has played a key role in promoting the worker cooperative model, and South Korea has also seen strong development of social cooperatives composed of different types of members (Eum, 2026).

Despite this progress, the Framework Act on Cooperatives did not fully resolve the institutional fragmentation facing the broader social economy. Different organizational forms remained governed by different laws, ministries, and programmes, creating inefficiency and redundancy across policy programmes (GSEF, 2026). Social enterprises, community businesses, and self-sufficiency enterprises each operated under separate legal frameworks, making it difficult to develop a coherent national strategy for the social and solidarity economy as a whole.

The Long Road to Comprehensive Legislation

The push for comprehensive SSE legislation began in 2014 when the Framework Act on the Social and Solidarity Economy was first proposed during the 19th National Assembly. Similar bills were repeatedly introduced in the 20th and 21st National Assemblies but expired without final passage (GSEF, 2026). This thirteen-year legislative journey reflected both the growing recognition of the SSE's potential and the political difficulties of building consensus around a new economic paradigm. The bills faced resistance from those who viewed the social economy as a marginal sector undeserving of dedicated national legislation, as well as from officials concerned about creating new bureaucratic structures.

The political context shifted significantly with the election of President Lee Jae-myung in 2025. Lee, a liberal president elected on a platform of economic and social justice, vowed to introduce the concept of a "social and solidarity economy" to South Korea, calling for the benefits of economic growth to be shared among all stakeholders as a way to address inequality (Korea Herald, 2025). Introducing legislation on the social and solidarity economy became one of 123 objectives outlined in the Lee administration's five-year policy blueprint. During a Cabinet meeting in Sejong, Lee stated that building a nationwide ecosystem to strengthen community solidarity for shared economic growth could be a game-changer, emphasizing the need to shift policy paradigms toward equitable and sustainable growth (Korea Herald, 2025).

The Framework Act on the Social and Solidarity Economy

On August 20, 2026, the National Assembly of the Republic of Korea passed the Framework Act on the Social and Solidarity Economy, marking a major milestone for the country's SSE (GSEF, 2026). The Act establishes, for the first time, a comprehensive national framework covering diverse SSE actors, including social enterprises, cooperatives, community businesses, self-sufficiency enterprises, and social ventures. It defines SSE as economic activities based on reciprocity, cooperation, and solidarity that pursue the common interests of community members and social value (GSEF, 2026). As the first comprehensive framework legislation on the social and solidarity economy in Asia and the Pacific, its adoption represents an important milestone for the region (UNSSE, 2026).

The passage of the Act followed the Comprehensive Plan for the Development of the Social and Solidarity Economy, jointly prepared by 20 government ministries and announced in June 2026 (GSEF, 2026). Together, the Comprehensive Plan and the Framework Act represent important steps toward establishing a coherent and sustained national policy framework for SSE in Korea. Under the Act, a Social and Solidarity Economy Development Committee under the President will coordinate national policy, and the government will establish a five-year Master Plan for the Social and Solidarity Economy to promote cooperation across ministries and between national and local governments (GSEF, 2026). The Act also formally institutionalizes social and solidarity finance, providing a better legal basis for patient capital and social investment, including loans and guarantees for SSE organizations.

Important Political Issues: Redistribution and the Citizen Dividend Debate

The social and solidarity economy has become entangled with broader political debates about economic redistribution in South Korea. In May 2026, a senior presidential official proposed a "citizen dividend" scheme that would return part of the windfall tax revenue generated by the semiconductor boom to the public as a way to address widening wealth inequality in the age of artificial intelligence (Korea Herald, 2026). The proposal sparked significant controversy, with critics arguing that the anti-market undertones contained in the concept of distributing profits in the form of dividends to every citizen were deeply concerning. From a corporate perspective, it was argued that profits should be directed toward securing future competitiveness rather than being dissipated through wasteful distribution (Korea Herald, 2026).

The debate over the citizen dividend reflects deeper tensions within Korean society about the relationship between economic growth and social equity. The government has also launched a public discourse process to discuss how to socially distribute the excess profits generated in the semiconductor industry, interpreted as a process to materialize the possibility of a "Korean-style social solidarity wage" (Business Korea, 2026). These debates occur against a backdrop of rising social inequality, labour market dualisation, and the proliferation of precarious employment alongside ultra-low fertility, challenges that present Korean society with profound social and economic difficulties (Fleckenstein & Lee, 2024).

Challenges Facing the Social and Solidarity Economy

Despite its institutional advances, South Korea's SSE faces significant structural challenges. An exploratory study on the concept and scalability of the social and solidarity economy found that throughout its administration-driven growth process, structural problems including distortion of social values, absence of active subjects, and institutional isomorphism have deepened (KCI, 2026). The rapid institutionalization and expansion of the SSE since the 2000s, led primarily by government initiatives, has created a tension between civil society autonomy and the government's policy coordination function (Discourse on the Social Economy, n.d.). There is a risk that SSE organizations become overly dependent on government support and lose their distinctive character as democratic, member-controlled enterprises.

The case of a government-led collaborative mobility platform in "City P" illustrates the limits of state-led digital solidarity economies. The initiative, framed as a "people-centred" project promising blockchain-enabled transparency and community co-ownership, experienced a "cascade of failures" across four dimensions: a state-led sociotechnical imaginary prioritized technological complexity over user needs; opaque "black-box" designs displaced community agency; participatory forums devolved into performative consultation; and appeals to traditional solidarity collapsed without visible reciprocity (Seo & Ammari, 2026). Despite official reports claiming measurable gains in jobs and traffic reduction, residents experienced friction and mistrust, with tensions escalating into over 1,500 complaints and local boycotts that eroded social capital. This case underscores that meaningful digital solidarity economies require enforceable governance rights, legible accounting, and culturally resonant ownership structures (Seo & Ammari, 2026).

The Broader Socioeconomic Context

The development of South Korea's social economy must be understood within the broader context of the country's socioeconomic challenges. South Korea currently faces the lowest birth rate in the world at 0.75, sky-high housing costs, growing mental health issues among young adults, and a collapsing ladder of social mobility (Korea Times, 2025). Regional provinces are hollowing out, small business closures have reached record highs, and a debt-ridden younger generation faces diminishing prospects. Labour market dualisation and the rise of insecurity have undermined the social fabric of the country in the absence of robust social protection mechanisms that could mitigate job insecurity and corresponding anxiety (Fleckenstein & Lee, 2024). Rising social inequality and the proliferation of precarious employment alongside ultra-low fertility present Korean society with profound challenges that call for an ambitious social and economic reform programme.

The SSE is increasingly viewed as a potential response to these challenges. Across Korea, SSE organizations are already developing community-based solutions in areas where various social problems have emerged, such as vacant property, climate crisis, lack of care services, and local unemployment (GSEF, 2026). The new framework is expected to strengthen the role of SSE in addressing challenges facing local communities, including inequality, regional depopulation, and mismatch of supply and demand in social services.

Conclusion

South Korea's social and solidarity economy has evolved from a marginal sector operating in the shadows of chaebol-led development to a legally recognized pillar of the national economic framework. The passage of the Framework Act on the Social and Solidarity Economy in 2026 represents the culmination of thirteen years of advocacy by policymakers, local governments, civil society, and SSE practitioners. Yet the institutionalization of the SSE brings new challenges, particularly the risk of government-led growth distorting social values and displacing genuine community agency. The success of Korea's social economy will depend not only on legal frameworks and financial support but on the ability of SSE organizations to maintain their democratic character and distinctive identity while scaling their impact. As the country confronts profound demographic and socioeconomic challenges, the social and solidarity economy offers a vision of economic organization that prioritizes human welfare and community resilience over purely quantitative growth.

title: The State of the Social Economy and Solidarity in Spain

article:
Introduction

The social economy in Spain represents a significant and growing part of the national economic landscape. It is a model of doing business that puts people and social goals ahead of pure profit. This sector includes cooperatives, mutual societies, foundations, associations, worker-owned companies, and other entities that follow specific principles. These principles include democratic management, prioritizing people over capital, and promoting solidarity both internally and with society at large (Law 5/2011, 2011). In Spain, this model is not a marginal phenomenon. It accounts for around 10% of the country's GDP and 12.5% of employment, making it a vital contributor to the economy and to social cohesion (Fundació Pere Tarrés, 2025).

Historical Background

The roots of Spain's social economy go back much further than the recent laws that regulate it. Cooperative and mutual aid traditions have existed for well over a century. Consumer cooperatives, for instance, developed in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, with Barcelona being a notable center of activity (Cambridge Core, 2021). However, the sector's growth was slower than in many other Western European countries for a long time (CIRIEC, 2024). A major turning point came during the economic crises of the 1970s and 1980s. During this period, thousands of workers who faced plant closures chose to take over their failing businesses and run them as cooperatives rather than lose their jobs. Between 1975 and 1985, around 1,300 factories in Spain were recovered by their workers in this way (Dumas, 2024). This era demonstrated the social economy's potential as a tool for resilience and job preservation during difficult times.

The Mondragon Example

Perhaps the most famous example of the social economy in Spain is the Mondragon Corporation, located in the Basque Country. Founded in the 1950s, Mondragon is now the world's largest worker cooperative group. It is an interconnected network of 92 cooperatives employing tens of thousands of people (ICA, 2026). Mondragon is known for its remarkably flat pay structure, where the highest-paid executives earn no more than nine times the salary of the lowest-paid workers, a stark contrast to the much larger gaps found in most conventional corporations (ICA, 2026). The group reinvests its profits into education, research, and social welfare institutions for its members, creating a deeply integrated and resilient ecosystem. Mondragon proves that a business focused on social benefit can also achieve major commercial success on a global scale (ICA, 2026).

Legal Recognition and Framework

A major milestone for the sector came in 2011 when Spain became the first country in Europe to pass a national law specifically on the social economy. Law 5/2011 established a common legal framework for all the various types of entities that make up the sector (Government of Spain, 2011). The law clearly defines the guiding principles of the social economy. These include the primacy of people and the social objective over capital, democratic and participatory governance, the application of profits in accordance with the work and services provided by members, and a commitment to solidarity, social cohesion, and the integration of people at risk of exclusion (Law 5/2011, 2011). This law was an important step in giving visibility and institutional support to a diverse set of organizations that had previously operated under separate legal rules.

The Sector in Numbers

The statistics paint a picture of a sector that is both large and diverse. According to the Spanish Business Confederation of the Social Economy (CEPES), the social economy is made up of around 43,000 companies and organizations that generate almost 2.2 million jobs (Fundació Pere Tarrés, 2025). The composition of these entities is varied. Cooperatives are the most common type, representing about 75% of the sector's companies. This is followed by fishermen's guilds, worker-owned companies, and integration companies (Fundació Pere Tarrés, 2025). In terms of employment, cooperatives alone employ over 330,000 people registered with the Social Security system (CIRIEC, 2026). The sector is especially strong in agriculture, but it also has a significant presence in services, construction, and industry.

A New Political Impetus

In recent years, the social economy has gained considerable political momentum under the Spanish government led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez. The Second Vice-President and Minister for Labour and Social Economy, Yolanda Díaz, has been a particularly vocal advocate. She has described the social economy as a "vaccine against inequality" and a tool for addressing structural problems like social exclusion and climate change (La Moncloa, 2025). The government has launched initiatives such as the State Network of Municipalities for the Social Economy, aimed at using the model as a lever for local development, especially in rural areas facing depopulation (Demócrata, 2026). This political focus has elevated the sector's profile both domestically and internationally.

Recent Legislative Developments

The political support has translated into new legislation. In March 2026, the Spanish Congress definitively approved the Comprehensive Law for the Promotion of the Social Economy (Law 1/2026). This new law aims to strengthen cooperatives and other entities, combat "intrusismo" or entities that falsely claim to be part of the social economy, and consolidate the sector's role in public procurement (Demócrata, 2026). The law was passed with the broad consensus of the sector's main representative organizations. However, it was not unanimously supported. The conservative Partido Popular (PP) and the far-right Vox party voted against it. The PP argued that the law was "confusing and ideological" and that it could have negative effects on cooperatives (Partido Popular, 2026).

Political Controversies and Tensions

The partisan divide over the social economy reflects the broader political polarization in Spain. While the left-leaning government promotes the social economy as a distinct and valuable alternative to traditional capitalism, the opposition parties view some of the government's initiatives with suspicion. The PP and Vox have focused their political discourse on a "national priority" agenda, which proposes giving Spaniards preferential access to public services and state aid over foreigners (The Local, 2026). Critics argue that this approach creates divisions and competes with the universal and solidarity-based principles of the social economy. These political tensions mean that while the sector has strong institutional support, it is also a subject of ongoing debate about its role and the broader direction of Spain's economic model.

Regional Diversity and Laws

One of the defining features of Spain's social economy is its strong regional dimension. The Spanish Constitution allows autonomous communities to legislate on cooperative matters, leading to a diverse legal landscape. Regions such as Aragon, the Canary Islands, Galicia, and La Rioja have enacted their own social economy laws (OECD, 2025). Catalonia is another key region, with a long-standing cooperative tradition. A proposed Law on the Social and Solidarity Economy has been debated in the Catalan Parliament since 2021, though it has yet to be approved (Wiley Online Library, 2026). This regional variability means that the specific rules, support policies, and even the terminology used to describe the social and solidarity economy can differ significantly depending on where an entity is located.

Ongoing Challenges and Criticisms

Despite its successes, the social economy in Spain faces several challenges. One concern is the marginalization and segmentation of the sector in certain urban contexts. Research in Barcelona has shown that even in neighborhoods with active promotion policies, social and solidarity economy entities can struggle to diversify and become truly embedded in the local economy (Wiley Online Library, 2026). There is also a risk of the sector being co-opted by public policy in a way that undermines its transformative potential. Furthermore, broader economic and social problems continue to affect the country. Issues such as a high youth unemployment rate, rising inequality, and a severe housing crisis create structural constraints that even a thriving social economy cannot single-handedly overcome (OECD, 2025; FEE, 2025).

International Projection

Spain has also positioned itself as a global leader in promoting the social economy. In 2026, following negotiations led by Spain, the first Ibero-American Commitment to the Social and Solidarity Economy (2026-2030) was adopted at a ministerial conference in Avilés (La Moncloa, 2026). This agreement is a significant milestone, as it represents the first major political consensus across the Ibero-American region on this issue. The Commitment sets out a roadmap for promoting public policies, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and using public procurement to support the social economy (La Moncloa, 2026). Spain also played a pioneering role at the United Nations, helping to secure the first UN resolution on the social economy, further cementing its international influence in this field (La Moncloa, 2026).

Conclusion

The state of the social economy and solidarity in Spain is one of growth, institutionalization, and political contestation. From its historical roots in mutualism and worker self-management to its current legal recognition and international advocacy, the sector has evolved into a substantial economic force. It offers a practical alternative to the dominant economic model, prioritizing people, democratic participation, and social goals. While it faces challenges related to internal segmentation, national political polarization, and the broader socio-economic context, its resilience is evident. The passage of new laws, the commitment to international cooperation, and the continued growth of cooperatives and other entities suggest that the social economy will remain a central and defining feature of Spain's socio-economic landscape for years to come.

title: The State of the Social Economy and Solidarity in America
